Experts told Carbon Brief that, strictly, the talks did not “collapse” as several negotiated items were still adopted. Rather, the rejection of the cover decision represented, for the first time, “those who want a higher level of ambition actively reject[ing] the lowest common denominator on offer”, said one veteran observer. Dispute over who would host COP31 – representing the “western Europe and other states” region – had gone on for three years . In the end, the two main rivals, Turkey and Australia, agreed to a deal last year at COP30 that the summit would take place in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia acting as “president of negotiations”. COP31 president and Turkish minister Murat Kurum and COP31 “president of negotiations” and Australian minister Chris Bowen. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis Critics questioned whether either country was well-placed to host, given their ongoing fossil-fuel expansion. Turkey faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields on the eve of the summit, while recent Carbon Brief analysis found that Australia is the third-largest CO2 exporter in history because of its fossil-fuel production. Ahead of the summit, the presidency released four official letters outlining a vision for COP31. The first letter , written by COP31 president Murat Kurum in April 2026, confirmed the appointment of Australian climate minister Chris Bowen as “president of the negotiations” and announced that a pre-COP would be held in Fiji in October. The second letter , authored by both Kurum and Bowen from the Copenhagen climate ministerial in May, said that “COP31 presents a vital opportunity to further accelerate…in the areas of clean energy, electrification and resilient infrastructure”. The third letter , published in August 2026, gave more details on the presidency’s plans for the “ action agenda ” – the part of the UN process that mobilises coalitions of nations and non-state actors to push climate action further. This letter also introduced a key aim from the presidency to get countries to agree to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 (often referred to as “35 by 35”). (See: Electrification .) The final letter , published in October ahead of the pre-COP in Fiji, said that the presidency would centre on “delivering a COP focused on accelerating implementation, electrification and resilience in an uncertain world”. It added that “many parties have emphasised the importance of reviewing and continuously improving UNFCCC processes, to ensure it remains fit for purpose, sustainable and focused as negotiations evolve over time”, adding: “At COP31, we will hold presidency consultations to hear parties’ views on how to strengthen UNFCCC processes, to ensure growing demands are met and to effectively deploy resources.” The pre-COP in Fiji was held from 5-8 October and was attended by 3,000 people. In this somewhat intimate setting, Bowen announced that Turkey and Australia had agreed to negotiate a “presidency-led” cover decision at COP31. He added that revealing this before COP was part of the presidency’s “upfront, transparent and consultative approach”. Later that month, the presidency named the five ministerial pairs from developed and developing countries that would take key negotiation issues forward at COP31. These issues were mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and oceans. COP31 kicked off on 9 November, with climate negotiations scholar (and Carbon Brief contributing editor ) Dr Joanna Depledge noting that it was clear from the summit’s opening ceremony that “Australia [was] the junior partner” in the presidency. COP’s opening day ran late into the night as the presidency worked to avert a fight over proposed changes to the summit’s negotiations agenda. Simon Evans 9 November 2026, 10:40 GMT COP31: Agenda adopted! Agenda adopted! Moments ago in Antalya, Turkey, COP31 president Murat Kurum outlined how an “agenda fight” has been averted, despite various proposals for additions to proceedings. This came after a short delay, while a series of huddles took place on… Read more on CB Connect → The next day, in plenary, Kurum announced that a resolution had been found. He said that calls for new agenda items on adaptation finance and trade were rejected, whereas an item on a new climate finance “work programme” had been added. (The EU expressed “deep concern” about the addition.) Kurum added that two extra proposed items on mountains and climate change – made more poignant by recent catastrophic floods in Nepal – were also not added to the agenda. However, he said that the presidency would instead hold consultations on the topic. Though an early scrap over the agenda was avoided, the summit’s opening days were plagued with logistical problems. Attendees were forced to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to get into the venue – sparking serious access concerns . A crowded roadbridge near the COP31 entrance in Antalya, Turkey. Credit: ZUMA Press, Inc. / Alamy Stock Photo The problems persisted into the first day of the world leaders’ summit on 11 November, when delegates were informed that they should travel between the hours of 5-7am to secure access to the venue. Ire only grew when security staff still let people in after this time. On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This was an “informal note” with a bullet-pointed list of topics that might be included. On Saturday evening, Kurum told a press conference that “around 30 countries” had indicated support for the 35 by 35 pledge. However, he had little to share on progress in the negotiations and eluded questions on how he planned to include “fossil fuels” in the cover decision. In the small hours of Sunday morning, half-way through the summit, Kurum announced presidency and ministerial consultations on “outstanding political issues”. He also invited ministers to a “divan” – a group meeting, not a daybed – to discuss cross-cutting issues. On Monday afternoon, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “ presidency note ” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text. (See: Cover decision .) At a press conference, Bowen told journalists that the presidency decided to release the text “early” to allow parties to debate on it for as long as possible and acknowledged that it would need to be “refined” down. On Wednesday evening, the presidency held its divan, where delegation heads sat in a circle and were asked to share their priorities for finding consensus in the negotiations. Countries take part in a “divan” at COP31. Credit: UNFCCC / Flickr Speaking at the divan, Kurum told parties that the second draft cover decision would be published that evening. In the end, the second draft cover decision was published on Thursday. Later that day, Kurum and Bowen spoke at a press conference, talking up their latest draft with lofty claims that it could “achieve [the] covenant of 1.5C and nothing more”. However, the second draft was rejected by countries and civil society alike. (See: Cover decision .) On Friday – the summit’s last scheduled day – the mood at COP soured. With few official updates, delegates relied on ever-changing rumours about when a new text might emerge. Negotiations on other key issues also remained stuck, as civil society dubbed it the “worst COP in history” at a press conference attended by Carbon Brief.  In the evening, the presidency opened the closing plenary to gavel through non-contentious items – and announced that a new text would not be released until Saturday morning.  They were interrupted by a protester wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” and with a red noose around their neck. As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update failed to arrive.  An open letter signed by 100 civil society organisations told the presidency it was “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UNFCCC has ever had”. As Turkish support staff started packing down the party pavilions, behind-the-scenes disputes between country ministers intensified. Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UK, the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the Independent Association of Latin America and the Caribbean (AILAC), the Umbrella Group (UG) and least-developed countries (LDCs) – approached the presidency as a united front to demand changes to the cover decision. These changes included on how it referenced transitioning away from fossil fuels, adaptation finance and carbon capture and storage. width: 64px; align-self: start; } } Membership Connect with our community Join CB+ A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.  With official updates still few and far between, rumours swirled that many countries were still not happy with this iteration of the text and planned to reject it. Later that day, another version of the text arrived – but it contained only minor changes. In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, several countries rejected the cover decision – citing reasons including its failure to respond to humanity’s overshoot of 1.5C of global warming, its failure to clearly mention fossil fuels and its lack of clear figures for adaptation finance. (See: Cover decision .) While countries rejected the cover decision, they did find consensus on other texts, including for the just transition work programme , the global goal on adaptation , the climate finance work programme , carbon markets , long-term finance and “Article 2.1c”. The final gavel came down at 7:33pm local time – nearly 50 hours after the summit’s scheduled end. This makes COP31 the longest in history.  Cover decision The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 countries during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious –  closing plenary in Antalya. Towards the end of the summit, Kurum had told a press conference attended by Carbon Brief that he wanted the cover decision to be known as the “Antalya accord”. (This was later amended in the last formal draft to be the “Antalya pact”.) But, in the closing plenary, the EU told the assembled delegates: “We will not endorse a cover decision, or an Antalya pact, that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” According to Carbon Brief’s tally during the closing plenary, the agreement was also explicitly rejected by Panama, the Marshall Islands, Belize, Norway and Vanuatu. After it was clear that the pact would not be adopted, the 44-member LDCs, the UK, South Korea and Japan all said that consensus had not been reached, a softer form of indicating dissent. The six-member environmental integrity group (EIG) also registered its “concerns” with the text. For months ahead of the summit, the Turkish and Australian presidencies had been talking up the idea of a COP31 cover decision – an overarching political statement. Indeed, Bowen had publicly raised the idea of a COP31 cover decision at last year’s COP30 in Brazil, even before the agreement to act as joint president with Turkey had been finalised. In his opening speech in Antalya, Bowen said that he had agreed with Kurum to take forward a “presidency-initiated, party-driven [cover] decision for COP31”. He had said at a pre-COP in Fiji: “There is a clear expectation that COP31 must respond to the global moment – to send a clear message to accelerate implementation…And to demonstrate our continued commitment to multilateralism, to international cooperation and to the Paris Agreement.” Bowen stressed that this should not lead to a “lengthy political statement”, but that he wanted it to respond to the imminent “ overshoot ” of 1.5C, the “catastrophic impacts” of warming and the “tangible progress” being made in the energy transition. For Turkey, the cover decision became a vehicle to promote what had started out as its voluntary target for electricity to make up 35% of global final energy by 2035. (See: Electrification .)  While early on, Russia publicly challenged the legal basis for a cover decision, given it was not on the official agenda, these procedural objections fell away as the summit continued. Many other recent COPs have issued cover decisions, setting a firm precedent . Carbon Brief understands that legal advice from the UNFCCC secretariat confirmed the broad authority of the presidency to initiate a cover decision in Antalya. Nevertheless, many parties remained unhappy about the existence of the cover decision, the process by which it was put together and the impact it had on time for other negotiations. For the LMDCs, India told the closing plenary: “We are also acutely aware that [the cover decision] has taken away our attention from the mandated items of the agenda, which we had to deliver.” It had quickly become clear that Bowen’s ambitions for a brief cover decision would be in vain, when a lengthy 144-paragraph “ reflections ” text was released on 16 November. Simon Evans 13 November 2026, 05:55 GMT NEW: COP31 cover decision ‘reflections’ text Today, Friday 13 November, the COP31 presidency published a “reflections” text on consultations it has been holding with heads of national delegations on a potential “cover decision”. This is not a fully formed draft text, but instead contains an organised… Read more on CB Connect → This document was a compilation of all the issues that parties had put forward for inclusion, ranging from quantified climate-finance goals through to firm timelines for the next assessment report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC). Other ideas included that developed countries should reach net-zero emissions by 2030, that certain trade policies should be “phase[d] out” next year and that the largely defunct Kyoto Protocol should be resurrected, with binding carbon targets for developed nations. The text also included the presidencies’ favoured “35 by 35” electrification target , as well as language on the transition away from fossil fuels. (See: Fossil fuels .) A second iteration – in reality, the first fully formed draft cover decision – was published on 19 November, consisting of just 80 paragraphs. This version was immediately criticised for having excised any mention of fossil fuels, as well as deleting the $120bn adaptation-finance target wanted by developing countries. (See: Adaptation .) It retained the “35 by 35” target, but only as one of a menu of options, listed as areas for “global cooperation” to “keep 1.5C within reach”. Paragraph 36 of the second draft cover text. Source: UNFCCC . Controversially, this menu of options – indicated by the wording “inter alia”, meaning “among other things” – also included numerical targets for carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS), apparently as “ quid pro quo ” for the quantified electrification target. The same day, in a highly unusual move, Panama issued an open letter stating that it would “formally object” to any decision not meeting demands including a “cap on oil production”. Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro. A third and supposedly “final” version of the cover decision was published at around 3am local time on Sunday 22 November, already deep into overtime at the summit. This still did not make any direct reference to fossil fuels or the $120bn adaptation finance target. It also removed language that had called for the next IPCC reports to be published ahead of the second “global stocktake”. Carbon Brief has seen proposed revisions presented to the presidency by a 126-nation coalition of countries, including the EU, LDCs, AOSIS, AILAC, EIG and Umbrella groups. They asked for the paragraph above – numbered 36 in the second draft and 40 in the third – to be replaced with a direct link to the first global stocktake, which included the transition away from fossil fuels. (They did not suggest an explicit use of the words “fossil fuels”.) The group also wanted the sub-paragraph with numerical targets for CCUS to be deleted. However, a fourth and final version of the “Antalya pact”, published a few hours later, made only minor changes, softening language on CCUS to “increasing” rather than “accelerating”, while also weakening the language around the timeline for the next IPCC reports. On the last scheduled day of negotiations, Bowen had told journalists: “The world is wondering whether multilateralism can deliver. I think it can.” But the presidencies’ efforts to secure a cover decision were, ultimately, unsuccessful. The UK told the closing plenary: “What is before us is not commensurate with the urgency of overshoot, the scale of the climate crisis or the impacts already being felt…It is the lowest common denominator…[rather than presenting] bold collective ambition on climate action.” Not all parties were opposed to the Antalya pact. Ghana, for the African group, said it could support the decision, despite the lack of specificity on topics including adaptation finance and trade measures.
