Saudi Arabia, for the Arab group, said that they had continued to “engage constructively” on the cover decision, “despite all of the issues that were taken off the table”, including on finance and historical emissions . It also said: “We cannot reconcile a position that stated so publicly that we need to keep 1.5C within reach and, yet, calling CCUS technologies greenwashing.” Russia explained its steadfast opposition to “any wording on fossil fuels” – despite the wording agreed by consensus at COP28. It criticised “slogans” around the use of fossil fuels, arguing that even in 1.5C pathways, there was an ongoing role for oil and gas. While the failure to adopt a cover decision has been widely compared to the collapsed Copenhagen climate talks in 2015, experts told Carbon Brief this comparison was flawed. Nevertheless, they said it could end the recent trend of COPs attempting to secure a cover decision, as well as sparking renewed reflections on how to reform the process. Paul Watkinson , the French chief negotiator at Paris COP21, told Carbon Brief: “This time it is the political bet of the presidency on a cover decision that has not worked…I think this needs a deeper reflection on what we are trying to achieve – there are limits to political signals in a decision – and we ought to think [about] what we can achieve through the COP and how to make it work better.” The failure of the Antalya pact meant that initiatives on oceans, methane, mountains – and on COP reform itself – were all lost from the formal outcome of the summit. While some may be revisited at future COPs, not all have a clear place on the agenda. COP reform As COP31 ended without agreement on the proposed “Antalya pact”, much of the immediate response focused on perceived shortcomings in the UN climate process. In his closing remarks , UNFCCC executive secretary Simon Stiell said there were “lessons that must be learned” for the consensus-driven process: “Clearly, there is also scope to improve, modernise and reform. But not only because of what happened here. But also because we must evolve in this era of implementation.” In fact, one of the COP31 presidency’s stated priorities had been reforming COPs – or what they described as “strengthen[ing] UNFCCC processes”.  COP reform was discussed during the summit, including at a press conference where Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro told journalists: “The COP has become an exercise in futility…192 countries will not agree on every single comma and every single period…especially those countries that produce carbon-based fuels.” In practice, such bombastic statements were far removed from the on-going discussions and country submissions on COP reform , which had already begun in Brazil last year.  These discussions were integrated into the formal negotiations under the heading of “ arrangements for intergovernmental meetings ” (AIM).  At the Bonn climate talks in June, Australia, along with Turkey, offered to conduct informal consultations on increasing UNFCCC “efficiency” at COP31.  The African group asked for legal clarity and cautioned that “efficiency should not be equated with reducing budgets or removing agenda items” necessary to tackle climate change, according to the Earth Negotiations Bulletin .  Early in the talks, the COP31 presidency published a concept note calling for “forward-looking and exploratory” discussions on what a “strong and effective UNFCCC process” could look like. It also initiated “presidency consultations” on the matter, despite the lack of a clear mandate for doing so. In the presidency consultations, responses included multi-year planning, retiring old agenda items and “avoiding unnecessary cover decisions”.  Several countries – including Russia, the African group, AILAC and the LMDCs – questioned the need for separate discussions and whether these were solely for the cover decision, given they were already underway in the AIM negotiations.  Russia said it “did not consent to elevating this discussion to high political level” and that it was unclear “why such a significant amount of negotiating time [was] being devoted” to these roundtables without a clear objective.  Drafts of the presidency’s failed cover decision included “high-level consultations” under COP presidencies on “strengthening the UNFCCC process”. During the final plenary, Peru, for AILAC, called for a “clear rule on votes” and an independent review of the COP process’s efficiency. Peru’s environment director Andrés Martín Garrido Sánchez said: “To negotiate in good faith is not a courtesy; it’s an obligation. It means not using delays as a strategy. It means negotiating text in the room in the view of everyone, with every party being heard before a decision is gavelled. It means not taking issues hostage…We are not proposing matters against the consensus. This way of negotiating is not leading us to where the world needs us to be.”  With the Antalya pact rejected, these discussions will still continue under AIM in Bonn in 2027. .cb-tweet img{ border: solid 1.25px #333333; border-radius: 5px; } @media (max-width:650px){ .cb-tweet{ width:100%; } } Adaptation While efforts to specify that tripling adaptation finance meant $120bn by 2035 failed to make it into any final texts, COP31 did see a breakthrough on channelling carbon-market revenues into the UN adaptation fund . Disagreements over finance dominated negotiations within the “ global goal on adaptation ” (GGA).  This followed a “call for efforts” to triple adaptation finance by 2035, which was agreed last year at COP30. That target was originally proposed by the LDCs as a “tripling of grant-based adaptation finance by 2030 to at least $120bn”.  Last year’s final agreement was considerably weaker and lacked key details – including the baseline for tripling and what kinds of funding would be counted towards it. Ahead of the start of COP31, the African group requested that the tripling goal be added to the agenda, providing a potential space to discuss these outstanding issues. African group request for agenda item on tripling adaptation finance. Source: UNFCCC . This request was rejected . As a result, the question of where the goal should be discussed quickly arose as a fault line. It was debated within the GGA, the climate finance “work programme”, as well as the proposed “cover decision”.  As negotiations got underway, the G77 and China coalition of developing countries argued that adaptation finance should be discussed in the GGA rooms.  The EU, UK, environmental integrity group (EIG), Norway and Canada all wanted adaptation finance discussed under the climate finance work programme. This would place the tripling goal within the broader $300bn target for 2035 – meaning adaptation finance could come from a wide variety of sources, not just developed-country grants. Over the first week of negotiations, two GGA draft texts were released, both of which included specific references to tripling adaptation finance to $120bn per year by 2035.  This would use a baseline of 2025, when the previous target to double adaptation finance to $40bn per year came to an end.  Draft GGA text on 13 November. Source: UNFCCC . Over the second week of COP31, parties continued to disagree over the home and baseline for the tripling target.  The first draft text on the cover decision – reflecting ideas put forward by parties – included relatively ambitious language that tripling finance for adaptation “should reach at least $120bn”. However, the “$120bn” was absent from the next draft and an accompanying GGA text . NGO network Climate Action Network (CAN) reported that France – as co-chair of the ministerial climate-finance negotiations – had proposed a 2019 baseline, which would reduce the tripling target to just $60bn a year by 2035.  For context, the latest UNEP report on adaptation suggests that developing countries will need a total of $305bn every year by 2035 to meet their adaptation needs. Ultimately, neither the GGA, the climate finance work programme nor the failed cover decision specifically contained a baseline or target figure for tripling adaptation finance. Bethan Laughlin , senior policy specialist at ZSL (Zoological Society of London), told Carbon Brief that the failure to agree a baseline does a “colossal amount of damage, because it is a continued betrayal of promises for finance of all types”.  Beyond finance, parties worked to establish an expert taskforce that could refine the set of 59 “indicators” for the global goal on adaptation, which had been agreed at COP30, as part of the two-year “Belém-Addis vision”. These are the metrics that countries will use to assess their progress in adapting to climate change. Speaking to Carbon Brief, Emilie Beauchamp , senior adaptation expert at International Institute for Sustainable Development ( IISD ), highlighted that the indicators had been pushed through in Brazil without full engagement from parties. She added:   “It ties into the bigger picture, which is that [the] Brazilian presidency’s cover decision didn’t leave any space for countries not to adopt these 59 indicators. These are complex and incomplete, which means most countries aren’t happy with them.” Parties agreed on the need for a “two-tier” approach to resolving this, with a taskforce undertaking technical work on the indicators and then a policy alignment process for testing them. However, the composition of the taskforce quickly became a sticking point, just as it had in Bonn earlier in the year, according to ENB .  The 19 November draft GGA text still contained three options on the taskforce’s composition, including a mix of experts nominated either by regions, the chairs of the UNFCCC subsidiary bodies or by UN organisations and other non-party stakeholders.  Parties also disagreed on references in the GGA text to the Paris Agreement and “common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities” ( CBDR-RC ), plus on recognition of the importance of the 1.5C goal in limiting the need for adaptation.  While the final decision agreed at COP31 does not mention overshoot or 1.5C, it does provide clarity on the taskforce. It “agrees” that six experts will be nominated per UN regional group, in addition to three experts nominated by the LDCs and three by small island developing states.  With so much time and focus given to the finance question, smaller technical aspects of the GGA negotiations struggled to find consensus across the two weeks of COP31.  Laughlin said:  “I think we are seeing these big-number finance issues as absolutely fundamental, but we’re also seeing the technical elements of the process, where the real work of implementation is done, be significantly challenged and, in my view, denigrated into obsolescence.” Observers told Carbon Brief that there had not been sufficient time given to the GGA, as well as items such as national adaptation plans (NAPs). One said that more than double the negotiating time had been devoted to the cover decision than to mandated items, such as the GGA, MWP and JTWP, over the first week.  Beauchamp told Carbon Brief she hoped that COP32 president Ethiopia would “break this pattern”.  Beyond the GGA, other adaptation items also proved challenging at COP31.  G77 and China huddle during informal consultations on national adaptation plans. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis. The adaptation fund is the oldest dedicated UN climate fund and was set up as part under the Kyoto Protocol. Now, it is in the process of transitioning to exclusively serve the 2015 Paris Agreement. This will allow it to access 5% of the revenues generated by the agreement’s Article 6.4 carbon market.  This process has previously been delayed by disagreements over the makeup of the fund’s board.  The expectation has been that under the Paris Agreement, the board would have set quotas for “developed” and “developing” nations – the terms used in the treaty – instead of  “Annex I” and “non-Annex I” nations, as it has done in the past.  Some parties see this distinction as important, because the UNFCCC annexes clearly separate a small group of predominantly European and industrialised states from other nations, whereas the “developed-developing” division is less clearly defined. Joe Thwaites , international climate finance director at Natural Resources Defense Council , told Carbon Brief that parties “can’t access” the Article 6.4 “share of proceeds” until this is resolved. A draft text released on 18 November continued to include references to both “developed countries” and parties “included in Annex I to the convention” within square brackets.  Ultimately, the final decision confirmed that there will be regional quotas instead of “developed” and “developing”, but it also confirmed that developing countries will continue to have a majority of seats on the board.  Thwaites described the resolution of the adaptation fund negotiations as “one bright spot” from the climate summit, noting: “The decisions at COP31 enable the fund to receive a share of carbon-trading proceeds under the Paris Agreement crediting mechanism, which will not be subject to the politics of national budget processes.”  Negotiations on NAPs , adaptation communications and adaptation committee discussions all ended with procedural conclusions, meaning no substantive agreement was reached.  One adaptation area with more progress was “matters relating to the LDCs”, an agenda item where parties discuss support and adaptation planning for the 44 LDCs .   Despite “difficult negotiations”, on the second Wednesday of COP31, parties agreed to a decision that establishes a “LDCs national adaptation plan implementation platform” under the LDCs expert group.  ENB quoted a delegate saying: “This decision may not make the headlines, but it means a lot for the more than one billion most vulnerable people who benefit from the work under this agenda item.” Finance As COP31 ended in disputes and finger-pointing, a major complaint by many parties was the failure to agree progress on climate finance. In their closing speeches, several developing-country figures expressed “profound concern”, accusing developed countries of “refusing to engage” on this “essential” issue.  Finance talks ended with little – beyond decisions to hold more meetings. There was no progress on “tripling adaptation finance”, despite efforts to flesh out this goal. (See: Adaptation .)  Finance negotiations took place amid major aid cuts by developed countries and, as revealed by Carbon Brief, a corresponding 70% drop in the amount of public climate funding being pledged. COP31 co-president Australia drew heavy criticism from NGOs for failing to commit new funds, along with other major donors, such as Germany, France and Japan.  Meanwhile, pledges to UN climate funds fell to their lowest levels in years, with few new commitments in Antalya.  Protesters at COP31 calling for climate finance. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . Two years ago, nations agreed on a “ new collective quantified goal ” (NCQG), which involves developed countries “taking the lead” in raising $300bn in climate finance a year by 2035. A variety of sources are expected to feed into this goal, including multilateral development banks , UN climate funds and private finance “mobilised” by public investments.  In recent years, roughly a third of total climate finance has been public finance from developed countries. The provision of funds by these nations now looks less certain , amid economic struggles and pressure to raise military spending. Developing countries, therefore, came to COP31 looking for assurances. Finance was discussed across most rooms in Antalya, but negotiations around a climate finance “ work programme ” – set up at COP30 last year – were the main venue for this push. Developing countries had wanted to create this space to discuss finance “provision” under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement, which says developed countries “shall provide” finance. This is taken to mean public funding – such as aid spending – from developed countries. (The NCQG, on the other hand, is a “mobilisation” goal, meaning it covers various funding sources, including private finance “mobilised” by public investments.) This came amid concerns that developed countries were trying to transfer responsibility onto others. Abdulkani Barrow , Somalia’s lead negotiator, told Carbon Brief: “Africa does not want developed countries’ historical financial responsibilities to become diluted by a general expectation that private investors, developing countries and other financial actors should provide the money.” However, due to pressure from developed countries, the work programme was set up with a broader remit, including Article 9.1 “in the context of Article 9…as a whole”.  Following initial talks in June, the programme was only added to the COP31 agenda due to a continued push by developing countries. The EU remained “deeply concerned” about its inclusion.   Coming into COP31, developing countries continued to insist that the work programme should focus exclusively on Article 9.1.  Some developing-country groups, notably the Like-Minded Developing Countries (LMDCs) and the Arab group , said it should consider ways to secure more from developed countries, including “burden-sharing arrangements”. They also argued for an extensive new set of talks and other activities. Extract from “work programme on climate finance” text from 15 November, showing an option for “burden-sharing arrangements”. Source: UNFCCC . Such ideas were unacceptable for developed countries, who generally wanted a far more limited set of actions that were “non-prescriptive” and “non-punitive”.  They argued that the talks should be based on the existing $300bn mobilisation goal, stressing that they were already contributing tens of billions a year. Prior to COP31, Wopke Hoekstra, European commissioner for climate, told Bloomberg that “any conversation on new fresh money is dead in the water”. (This statement – and choice of words – sparked outrage among civil society and was even quoted by India’s Amandeep Garg in the closing plenary.) Speaking at the climate summit, Hoekstra told Carbon Brief: “We made a deal with the whole world community on financing…We don’t think there is any merit in opening it.” (The work programme was established “without prejudging the process for the implementation of the NCQG”.) There were a few finance-related issues that the EU and their allies were happy to discuss, including “broadening the contributor base” to include wealthier developing countries. Developed-country groups also said they wanted the discussions about “ tripling adaptation finance ” to take place within the work programme, as part of the NCQG. This would mean adaptation finance coming from both their public spending and other sources . In particular, the EU, the UK and others said they wanted to discuss “access” – helping small islands and other low-capacity nations to better get hold of the finance that already exists. Ilana Seid , chair of AOSIS, told Carbon Brief that this focus on access presented small-island states with “an interesting dilemma”, because they also needed more finance, noting: “The whole machinery needs to move.” The developed countries’ stated focus on access amounted to little, with no mention in the final finance decision . The Australian presidency was set to launch an “ access declaration ” for small islands and LDCs at COP31 – but the event was cancelled, partly due to lack of signatories. After drafts circulated , the first official work programme text landed at the start of the second week. It contained two lengthy, opposing sets of “options”, which broadly reflected the competing priorities of the developed and developing-country blocs. Josh Gabbatiss 16 November 2026, 08:50 GMT NEW: First official climate finance text drops The first official draft of text for the climate finance “work programme” has just dropped. There are major divisions between developed and developing countries, including over whether the programme has already started. It follows a proposed text that was being… Read more on CB Connect → The EU, Switzerland and New Zealand reportedly argued that a “no text” option should be on the table. This was reflected in the next iteration , which had a set of brackets around the entire document.  NGOs said the EU was acting as a “ villain ”. Sehr Raheja , deputy programme manager at the Centre for Science and Environment , told Carbon Brief: “If they’re derailing the negotiations on this work programme, then that commitment to the NCQG – in my mind – is questionable.” Co-chairs of the finance negotiations attempted to combine the work-programme discussions with another set of talks on Article 2.1c of the Paris Agreement – which relates to “making finance flows consistent” with climate goals.  Developing countries objected to this effort. They wanted to keep discussions focused on the responsibilities of developed countries, rather than broadening them to all “finance flows”. As COP31 drew to a close, it became clear that a stripped-back outcome was likely for both the work programme and Article 2.1c negotiations, with nothing substantial on finance provision, tripling adaptation finance or any other stated party priorities. This was reflected in the final decisions , which contained largely procedural outcomes. Notably, parties did agree to continue discussing finance under the work programme until 2028, rather than ending next year as some developed countries preferred . Less high-profile finance texts, such as the Standing Committee on Finance , also finished with largely procedural outcomes.  Just transition work programme Discussions on how to create a new “ just transition mechanism ” (JTM) proved one of the most controversial aspects of COP31 and were, ultimately, deferred to COP32.  At COP30 last year, negotiations under the broader “just transition work programme” (JTWP) had agreed to launch the mechanism, a decision seen as a key “ legacy ” of the summit. At COP31, parties were expected to agree on the form and function of the mechanism, to allow it to start working.  Following work in Bonn in June and a workshop in Sydney in the autumn, parties began negotiations in Antalya productively, with general consensus emerging on a two-tier structure for the mechanism. This would include a political and governance body, as well as a technical operational arm, according to Earth Negotiation Bulletin (ENB). Similarly, despite some divergences on the duration and scope of the work programme, there was broad support for the continuation of the JTWP beyond 2026. This initial work suggested that the JTM – referred to as the Belem-Antalya Mechanism (BAM) by civil society – would have a similar format to that previously suggested by NGOs and academics.  However, a draft text prepared at the end of the first week of negotiations was met with criticism from civil society, due to its lack of substantive detail on the mechanism.  They told Carbon Brief in statements that it was “hollow”, “watered-down” and an “insult to the principles parties agreed in Brazil”, adding that the “exciting potential for COP31 to deliver a real just transition mechanism is hanging by a thread”.  Speaking to Carbon Brief, Dr Leon Sealey-Huggins , a senior campaigner at the charity War on Want , said there had been a “steep decline” in negotiations.  He added that developed parties, such as the EU, Norway and the UK, were pushing for the mechanism to run dialogues, produce reports and connect people. He said that while this was “fine”, it is largely already happening in the JTWP and would have little impact on implementation.  Sealey-Huggins continued: “G77 and China have been really strong on pushing back on that in various different ways. [They are] united in the call for some kind of institutional arrangement that will have longevity, that will have power to implement work and that will do the work of scaling up means of implementation [and] support.”  Over the second week, the key areas of focus became who would set up and run the mechanism, the involvement of non-party stakeholders and how it would be financed. The G77 and China, African group and LDCs shared proposals on how the mechanism could deliver implementation. The EU and EIG highlighted the role of non-party stakeholders. Anabella Rosemberg , senior advisor on just transition at NGO umbrella group CAN International , told Carbon Brief that the arrival of ministers in the second week put a “cold wind in our room”. She said that what should have been a “relatively easy win” for COP31 was disrupted by disagreements in other areas, including finance and mitigation. Throughout the second week, there was also criticism of the Turkish presidency’s involvement in the JTWP. On 17 November, it was given a “dishonourable mention” in CAN’s “ fossil of the day ” award. This followed COP31 president Murat Kurum saying during a ministerial roundtable:  “Rather than creating new structures, it would be more favourable to establish a system that better connects existing resources.” Parties and civil society were quick to criticise the statement, which they viewed as breaching presidential neutrality.  As the summit progressed, negotiations became further mired in disagreement. Rosenberg told Carbon Brief they were hampered by the focus on the cover decision, which “basically captured the oxygen of the negotiations”.  On 19 November, a new JTWP draft text was published. However, the entire body of it was contained within square brackets. Key issues, such as the institutional arrangements for the new mechanism, were still only mentioned as “options”.  A call from the G77 and China for the mechanism to be a “constituted body”, meaning a specialised subsidiary that would house work on the mechanism would be established under the UNFCCC, was not included, observers told Carbon Brief.   Civil society – who originally proposed the mechanism – became increasingly vocal as COP31 moved into its final scheduled day. At a packed press conference attended by Carbon Brief, speakers said it had been “possibly the worst COP in history” and that they “unequivocally reject” the outcomes as they stood. Molly Lempriere 20 November 2026, 16:13 GMT Civil society hits out at ‘terrible COP’ that is ‘abject failure’ As we await new draft texts for the cover decision, just transition work programme, global goal on adaptation and more at COP31, civil society has just held a hectic press huddle to condemn the lack of process here in Turkey.… Read more on CB Connect → The final decision , published late on 21 November, sets out a phased approach to setting up the new just-transition mechanism.  It says that in Bonn next year, parties will work out what the mechanism will do and how it will work, with a view to this being formally agreed at COP32 in Ethiopia in November 2027. In a statement, Gina Cortés Valderrama , political strategist at 350.org said civil society and developing countries “stood firm in the face of a weak” mechanism, which “rich nations were trying to throw over the edge”. She added:  “Damage control is not a victory at this point. This is a failure of ambition and leadership, particularly from the so-called ‘developed countries’, who obstruct the provision of support, and of the COP31 presidency, who sidelined the united calls from 135 countries – almost 80% of the global population.” Beyond the mechanism, parties discussed a review of the JTWP and the key messages that emerged from the fifth and sixth just-transition “dialogues” held in 2026. Over the two weeks of negotiations, parties disagreed on language around agriculture and other topics, as well as the inclusion of references to transitioning away from fossil fuels and trade – neither of which made it into the final decision.  At COP30 last year, references to minerals had been included in earlier drafts on the JTWP – the first time they had appeared in a text within the UNFCCC process. However, this did not make it into the final decision in Belém.  At COP31, “critical minerals” were referenced in a COP decision for the first time.  In a statement, Angela Asuncion , Asia-Pacific coordinator and transition-minerals focal point at the Resource Justice Network , welcomed the inclusion as a “notable step”, but added that “the decision by parties to eliminate human rights due diligence across critical mineral supply chains is unacceptable”. She added:  “Stripping away these fundamental safeguards is a profound failure of leadership. By failing to operationalise the BAM and removing human-rights safeguards in critical-mineral operations, governments have once again abandoned frontline communities.” Loss and damage Negotiations on “ loss and damage ” resulted in few substantial outcomes at COP31 and only limited recognition of the gap in funding to aid victims of climate disasters. On top of finance to support emissions cuts and climate adaptation, developed countries are expected to take the lead on this issue. Loss-and-damage funding has been particularly in the spotlight since the devastating Himalayan floods over the summer. The Nepali government subsequently requested $20m from the UN fund for loss and damage , which was established with much fanfare at COP27 in 2022. So far, predominantly developed nations have pledged just $342m to the fund, a fraction of the $2.8bn in funding requests that developing countries have submitted. The fund’s board does not plan to start distributing finance until December, despite pressure to begin fast-tracking applications in response to urgent needs. Speaking at a COP31 side event , Nepali environment minister Gita Chaudhary said “disasters do not wait for the paperwork and neither can survivors”. She added: “The gap between the scale of loss and damage and the resources available in the fund is enormous and growing, so Nepal, therefore, strongly urges developed country parties to honour their commitments.” Gita Chaudhary, environment minister of Nepal, at COP31. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis . Unlike previous years , very little new loss-and-damage funding was announced at COP31 – limited to €15m ($16.5m) from Spain , plus Italy and the EU formalising previous pledges. The fund’s first replenishment process is due to start in 2027. In negotiations, parties were tasked with discussing a report on the loss and damage fund and deciding what guidance – if any – they wanted to provide for its operation.  Explaining why such guidance might be necessary, Liane Schalatek , an associate director and climate-finance expert at Heinrich Böll Stiftung , told Carbon Brief: “From developing countries, there have been concerns about things that are happening in the board meetings…There is no sense of urgency from developed countries to figure out how and when we do resource mobilisation.” An initial text presented two options. The first – favoured by the African group, LDCs and AOSIS – laid out six pages of guidance for the fund, “noting with concern” the gap between funding available and requests made. The alternative, supported by the EU and Japan, simply stated “no guidance”. They cited concerns about “ micromanaging ” the fund’s board. The final text “noted” the loss-and-damage finance shortfall, but contained relatively weak language about the need to scale up funding. One exception was a line “urg[ing] the conversion of pledges as soon as possible”, referring to promised funds that have not yet been paid out. Meanwhile, there were technical discussions at COP31 involving the joint annual report of the executive committee of the Warsaw International Mechanism (WIM) and the Santiago Network , plus the governance of the WIM. These two bodies are involved in research and helping developing countries access technical assistance to deal with loss and damage. One key dispute in these negotiations concerned WIM governance, which has gone unresolved for several years , but has not prevented the body from undertaking its work.  In the end, parties decided to simply defer the issue again, with a footnote in the final decision stating that this does not “prejudge outcomes” on WIM governance. Gender There was limited progress on negotiations on gender in Antalya, as a small number of parties once again pushed back on language on inclusion.   At COP30 last year, parties agreed on the Belém gender action plan (GAP), which set out specific actions for ensuring gender-responsive climate action and indicators for measuring parties’ progress on gender-related issues. This year’s summit was expected to be a “simple procedural negotiation”, with parties meant to discuss several reports that were deliverables under the GAP, said Bridget Burns , executive director of the Women’s Environment and Development Organization (WEDO).  However, she told Carbon Brief: “Our experience has shown us that even the most insignificant procedural negotiations can also get quite derailed and that’s somewhat what happened here.” During the first consultations, on 10 November, the co-facilitators sought parties’ views on three reports prepared by the secretariat, according to Earth Negotiations Bulletin (ENB).  ENB said that several negotiating groups used their time to highlight the need for finance, capacity-building and technology transfer in order to effectively implement the GAP. The first draft of the text, released late that day, “welcome[d]” the three reports and the work conducted under the GAP during its first year. It also “t[ook] note” of a report on addressing reported cases of harassment at the UNFCCC, but did not significantly mention the need for additional means of implementation. On the second day of consultations, the G77 and China reportedly asked for stronger language on finance, which was reflected in brackets in the text’s second draft , as shown below. A paragraph recognising the need for support for developing countries to implement gender action. Source: UNFCCC . Later in the first week, several parties objected to the use of inclusive language. They also disagreed over whether they should “welcome” or “take note” of the secretariat’s reports. (The latter is considered to be weaker language .) As at last year’s summit, Argentina, Paraguay, Russia and the Holy See – the government of the Vatican – raised objections over the use of previously agreed, gender-inclusive language in the draft.  Burns told Carbon Brief that it was “continually jarring” to see the Holy See “huddling with Russia in almost every negotiation stream”. She added: “The Holy See has been specifically vocal in these negotiations…and, in my opinion, [are] disastrously using the moral capital that they have to drive this process into procedural negotiations that are meaningless to actually changing what has been [previously] adopted in this process.” The final text , published on 14 November, reflected the lack of consensus, simply saying that the SBI had “considered” the reports and “acknowledged” the work being done to implement the GAP. Noemi Grütter , head of advocacy and partnerships at the Global Alliance for Green and Gender Action , told Carbon Brief that, despite the lack of progress on the agenda item, important work on implementation is still happening on the ground. She added: “There is also the reality that we need to build power outside of UNFCCC, because it’s not fast enough. There are countries that are willing [to do that], and I think we need to work with them.” According to the Guardian , Argentina and Paraguay both intervened over the definition of gender in the plenary during the adoption of the standing finance committee decision in the early hours of Sunday morning. Article 6 Negotiations at COP31 on carbon trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement reopened many familiar arguments over how tightly such activities should be regulated. Beatriz Granziera , senior policy adviser at The Nature Conservancy (TNC), told Carbon Brief: “Discussions repeatedly came back to familiar trade-offs: practicality versus conservativeness; flexibility versus oversight; and how to scale much-needed participation and investment while maintaining environmental integrity.” Agreement was, ultimately, reached on both bilateral trading under Article 6.2 and the international carbon market under Article 6.4. Carbon trading between countries under Article 6.2 is only subject to light-touch rules, such as reporting on the use of the process and a “technical expert review” of national reports. Across 16 national reports checked so far, these reviews found 543 “inconsistencies”, 115 of which were “significant”. None of the reports were found to be without issue. An initial draft text at Antalya “note[d these issues] with concern”, adding that “many…are significant” and relate to “environmental integrity” – in other words, whether or not emissions are actually being cut. It asked parties to address issues “at the earliest opportunity”. However, this entire paragraph disappeared in the final, agreed text . Instead, the decision “takes note” of the information in the technical reports, without asking for any response. Given its confidentiality provisions, campaign groups have long described Article 6.2 as a “ wild west ” for carbon trading and the COP31 outcome does nothing to tighten the rules. Separately, parties were unable to reach agreement at COP31 on how to fund the processes needed to run Article 6.2. Instead, they agreed to continue discussions next year, requesting a technical paper on how “fees or other funding arrangements” would work. On Article 6.4, negotiations began against a backdrop of calls for a “ course correction ” on the way the international carbon market is operated. This came in an open letter from the Project Developer Forum and the International Emissions Trading Association (IETA), saying market rules were too “conservative”. Andrea Bonzanni , senior director at IETA, told Carbon Brief that the “current version of [the market] is failing to attract investment in carbon projects”. The requests in the open letter appeared in early draft text, after being taken up by the like-minded developing countries and others. A 14 November draft “request[ed]” the supervisory body to “assess the cumulative impact” that its rules and standards have on the “feasibility” and “cost” of carbon-credit schemes. It said this was to avoid “excessive compounding of conservative adjustments”, in what amounted to asking that the rules for the Article 6.4 market not be too stringent. Draft text of 14 November on Article 6.4. Source: UNFCCC . Isa Mulder , at Carbon Market Watch , told Carbon Brief that this looked like market proponents “chipping away at the standards that have been set out”. She added: “The goal [of Article 6] was to enable higher ambition, not to enable [carbon-trading] activities.” However, after pushback from the EU and others, the final text adopted at COP31 no longer asks for a formal assessment of the “cumulative impact” of the rules. Instead, it asks that the supervisory body “take into account” the way different standards “operate together” when making or revising provisions. Towards the end of the summit, 45 scientists signed an open letter saying that the Article 6 rules “must be consistent with the science”. With those rules set for a review starting in 2028, Granziera told Carbon Brief: “Ultimately, the debate [at COP31] reflected different views on what is needed for Article 6 to deliver more effectively as a tool for achieving the goals of the Paris Agreement, which will likely come back to light in 2028.” Agriculture and food security For the second year in a row, negotiations on the Sharm el-Sheikh joint work on agriculture (SJWA) collapsed without parties reaching an agreement.  SJWA is where formal negotiations around climate change and agriculture take place under the UNFCCC.  Part of SJWA’s mandate is to synthesise information about work being done in the agricultural space – under both the UNFCCC and other international bodies – in an annual report.  SJWA also held two workshops – one on holistic approaches to agriculture and one on “means of implementation”, usually taken to mean finance – where countries and other partners could share their experiences, as captured in summary reports. At this COP, parties were meant to discuss the conclusions of these reports and, time permitting, decide on the future of the agricultural workstream under the UNFCCC. (The four-year mandate of SJWA was set to end at COP31.) Many observers were hopeful of agreeing a text that recognised agroecology as beneficial for humans, climate and biodiversity.  However, in the first negotiating session, on 10 November, the Arab group expressed its view that fertilisers are vital for food security and fertiliser exports are being impacted by the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM). Therefore, it said, the agriculture talks needed to discuss CBAM and other trade measures. Teresa Anderson , global climate-justice lead at ActionAid , called this a “total curveball” in the negotiations. She told Carbon Brief: “Everybody’s faces just dropped…Suddenly we knew that the chances of agroecology having a chance had been pretty elegantly spiked by putting in this really complicated political issue into the middle of the agriculture discussions.” Other observers also expressed frustration to Carbon Brief that the group had brought CBAM into the negotiations, noting that trade measures are being discussed elsewhere in the COP.  At the end of this session, parties were asked to submit their views in writing for consideration, with the LMDCs proposing an extension of SJWA to COP32.  A draft text circulated on the evening of 12 November – after the scheduled start of the negotiations that evening – left many parties unsatisfied, with several stating that elements of the text crossed their “red lines”. The draft presented parties with four options, including “no text”. Options for SJWA presented in a draft text on 12 November. Source: UNFCCC . Although various parties objected to many parts of the proposed text – including agroecology (opposed by India), CBAM (opposed by the EU) and “food systems” language (opposed by the G77) – the underlying issue was a lack of finance, observers told Carbon Brief. Marie Cosquer , advocacy analyst at Action Against Hunger , said:  “The main issue is not bad-faith negotiating; it’s the fact that across the UNFCCC, the countries that have a climate debt are not paying it…Unless they move on finance, there is nothing in this negotiation for global south countries.” With no sight of agreement on the horizon and the scheduled negotiating time drawing to a close, parties suggested that the negotiations end with a procedural text. The co-facilitators put such a text forward on 14 November. This final text says only that parties “continued consideration” of SJWA and have “requested the subsidiary bodies to continue consideration” of SJWA at the mid-year intersessional meetings in Bonn. The subsidiary bodies are then “requested” to report back at COP32.  Mitigation work programme The “mitigation work programme” (MWP) stalled repeatedly over the two weeks of COP31, and was ultimately blocked in the closing plenary, with work pushed back to Bonn in 2027.  The MWP – the only formal agenda item at the annual COP that is specifically focused on cutting greenhouse gas emissions – was set to come to an end in 2026. As such, parties have been wrangling with an existential question over the past year – both regarding the continuation of the programme and what it should work on. Both in Bonn and at COP31, divisions arose over the challenge of ensuring the MWP is “facilitative and non-prescriptive and…drive[s] greater urgency on mitigation ambition and implementation”, as the Center for Climate and Energy Solutions noted . At the Bonn intersessional meetings in June, countries were unable to agree on how to balance these two aspects and negotiations were subject to “ rule 16 ”, meaning there was no outcome and discussions were knocked over to the next session.   In the run-up to COP31, submissions from parties made it clear that there was support for the continuation of the programme.  According to Earth Negotiations Bulletin (ENB), as negotiations got underway on 10 November, parties diverged on the duration of the programme – with suggestions including out to 2030 or 2040 – and on a review of the purpose of MWP.  Additionally, Switzerland proposed establishing a permanent mitigation committee that would be similar to standing bodies in other areas of the UNFCCC process. This was opposed by the Arab group. .cb-tweet img{ border: solid 1.25px #333333; border-radius: 5px; } @media (max-width:650px){ .cb-tweet{ width:100%; } } Speaking to Carbon Brief, Lola Vallejo , diplomacy and partnerships director at the European Climate Foundation (which funds Carbon Brief) and former co-chair of the MWP, said the proposal raised an “interesting question”.  She noted that, alongside the climate finance “work programme”, there is a standing committee focused on finance, but there has not been one proposed for mitigation previously.  Vallejo added that while finance discussions may not be “getting the political traction” many wanted at COP31, “at least there’s no shortage of spaces to discuss”, unlike mitigation, which solely has the work programme. Observers told Carbon Brief that there was pushback against this proposed mitigation committee, on the basis that there is not a lack of institutions or bodies to tackle the issue, rather, there is a lack of finance and support. Areas of divergence between parties included connection (or not) to the “ global stocktake ”, connection to NDCs or other collective goals, mentions of the IPCC and to what extent the “action agenda” can be brought in, according to Vallejo.  Various designs for the continuation of the MWP were proposed in subsequent negotiations, including multi-year work plans and introducing more “focused, solutions-oriented global dialogues” to facilitate implementation. The extent of the disagreements was evident in a draft text published at the end of the first week of COP31, which contained 177 square brackets and 12 “options”.  In the second week in Antalya, progress continued to stall in the MWP negotiations. A new draft text released on 18 November highlighted that the duration of the programme, links to the global stocktake (GST) and the potential for a committee remained contentious.  While it was cut down from the previous iteration, this was, in part, because contentious issues had been replaced by placeholders without any content, as shown below. Draft text for the MWP, published 18 November. Source: UNFCCC . Natalie Jones , senior policy advisor on energy at the International Institute for Sustainable Development , told Carbon Brief that some parties were pushing to weaken language around the MWP’s original mandate to “accelerate action in this critical decade”, as well as language linking the work programme to the GST. She said:  “Some parties want to limit what the GST can say on mitigation. Basically, they want to avoid another sort of transitioning away from fossil fuels (TAFF) situation at COP33 and avoid any more top-down or sectoral targets or whatever, and they fear that they could come out of the MWP into the stocktake.” The next day, another draft text was published. This was close to agreement, with just two outstanding options: whether the MWP should take into account any “mitigation-related outcomes” of each stocktake when planning its activities or dialogues, or to have no text on the matter.  The draft text “decides” that one global dialogue will be held every year from 2028 under the MWP, leaving the door open for additional in-person or hybrid dialogues. Furthermore, it decides that the work programme will be extended until the end of 2030 and be renamed the “Sharm el-Sheikh-Antalya mitigation ambition and implementation work programme”.  Speaking to Carbon Brief, Fernanda de Carvalho , head of policy for climate and energy at WWF International , said the continuation of the MWP would be “better than nothing”, but added the process needed to be “significantly strengthened to deliver on its mandate”.   She added:  “A few parties keep pretending the link between this process and the GST doesn’t exist; they should just look at the decision that created the MWP.” Despite a clean text being released on 21 November – with the reference to the Paris Agreement removed from the preamble, but the reference to the GST remaining – parties failed to adopt the MWP in the closing plenary. Saudi Arabia and Russia both rejected the programme there, with the former stating it was “deeply disappointed by the continued attempts throughout these negotiations to fundamentally alter the facilitative, non-prescriptive and bottom-up nature of the mitigation work programme”. It said parties had tried to “move it away from its agreed mandate”. The UK, for the Umbrella group, lamented that the MWP could not be agreed, adding that the “complementarity of the global stocktake has been part of the MWP mandate from the beginning”. With no agreement in Antalya, work on the MWP will be pushed to Bonn in 2027, with the future of the programme uncertain. Response measures Talks on “response measures” were some of the least contentious at COP31, however, the final plenary still rejected a draft decision on the topic.  At UN climate talks, “ response measures ” is a forum for discussing the effects of carbon-cutting policies on countries. They are particularly relevant for nations where controls on emissions or deforestation pose a risk to communities and the economy.  In recent years, the forum has been where trade and climate issues have been discussed.  In 2024, COP29 in Baku established a four-year work plan on response measures, including the “cross-border impacts” of climate-change measures. This created a formal space to discuss and assess trade-related climate measures in UN climate talks.  COP30 in Belém established a two-day “global dialogue” on response measures each year from 2026-29. The first was in Bangkok from 21-22 September 2026, focusing on economic diversification and on how to manage impacts on vulnerable populations. COP31 also conducted its first annual ministerial high-level round table on response measures on 17 November. Credit: Kubilay Ciftci / UNFCCC In Antalya, three key disputes emerged. The first was on what activities the forum would undertake in 2027 and, second, how it would consider recommendations from its Katowice Committee (KCI) of experts. The third was on whether – and how – response measures would inform the second “ global stocktake ”. At the start of negotiations, countries – including the African group, AOSIS, South Korea and China – called for a wide range of activities next year. One of these included a new “cross-border” impact assessment of response measures. On 16 November, the EU suggested removing an activity that refers to Article 3.5 of the 1992 UN climate convention, covering trade and an “open international economic system”.  Eventually, countries settled on four different activities. These include a workshop next June for the most affected countries to learn how to report these impacts, plus another workshop at COP32 on “technological solutions” to reduce climate impacts. As work on the second global stocktake (GST2) gets underway, countries disagreed on how response measures would feed into it. As of 19 November , the same four options remained on the table, including one with “no text”.  One option, supported by G77 and China, “decide[d]” that all of the outputs of the forum – dialogues, workshops, technical reports and case studies – would serve as substantive inputs to GST2.  This option “urged” that the cross-border impact assessment be conducted “before and during” GST2, including metrics such as inflation, trade flows, household income, employment and debt. Canada and the EU warned that this would change the global stocktake’s “well-established function”, reported Earth Negotiations Bulletin .  However, Switzerland, Norway, EU and the UK supported a compromise option – where countries could submit their views on the “social and economic impacts of response measures” as input to GST2.  Eventually, the option explicitly containing a cross-border impact assessment as an input to  GST2 was deleted from the final draft .   Instead, the text “recognises” that inputs to GST2 are “non-exhaustive” and “affirms” that all the forum’s outputs will feed into the stocktake’s technical assessment. This includes work on cross-border impacts – including trade measures – and how to report and analyse them. At the same time, it “invites” countries to submit their views on the “social and economic consequences” of response measures by 28 February 2027, which would also inform the stocktake. During the final plenary, the EU told delegates it objected to the adoption of the decision on response measures, on the grounds that it “contains provisions that are highly problematic”, as well as “the lack of recognition of the best available science”.  This was supported by Canada and the UK, with the latter adding: “We cannot accept any outcome that seeks to undermine and unduly influence the next global stocktake.” Brazil and Saudi Arabia both expressed their disappointment with the rejection of the text. Brazil said that the draft “excludes the voices of developing countries, the very countries that struggle to address the social and economic impacts of mitigation measures”. It asked for a formal note that the role and mandate of the forum were being “undermined”. Action for climate empowerment A draft decision on “ action for climate empowerment ” (ACE) had been set for adoption at COP31, but was unexpectedly torpedoed by Russia in the closing plenary. This area of the negotiations aims to encourage people to engage in climate action in different ways – through education, training, public awareness and access to information. COP27 had agreed to a four-year “action plan” on ACE that ends this year. COP31 was due to have agreed a new plan for 2027-2031, with some parties wanting it to address “misinformation and disinformation” related to climate change. During the Antalya talks, Russia, along with Saudi Arabia and Paraguay, objected to including a reference to countering climate-related “misinformation and disinformation”, reported ENB . It added that Russia described this as amounting to the censorship of other scientific views. Russia also made repeated efforts to replace previously agreed language on “gender-responsive” action with the phrase “gender-sensitive”. A draft decision , proposed by the presidency on 21 November, “note[d] the need to enhance efforts to promote and support the integrity of information on climate change”. The proposal also “recognise[d] the centrality of equity and the best available science for effective climate action and policymaking, as provided by the IPCC”. It then set out an action plan for continued work from 2027-2031. Notably, while references to “misinformation” had been removed, it still talked of “ensuring that the public has access to reliable, accurate climate information and is equipped with adequate climate literacy skills”. Draft text for the ACE “action plan”, published 21 November. Source: UNFCCC . During the closing plenary, however, Russia said it “reject[ed]” the “censorship of science” and that it “objected” to the draft text on action for climate empowerment. It said discussions had been “held hostage by considerations which are not part of the climate process”. The EU and the UK for the Umbrella group expressed their “surprise” at Russia’s objection. The UK said this topic was “very important for our group” and that “respect for gender equality and all identities is core to an effective, inclusive and meaningful process”. The COP president told the plenary that, “in light of the objection from the Russian Federation”, the issue of action for climate for empowerment would be deferred until the Bonn talks in June 2027. In a statement, campaign group Climate Action Against Disinformation said: “The ACE action plan should have been a milestone for truth at COP31. Instead, the Russian federation – the epicentre of climate disinformation – blocked its adoption, standing alone against 193 other[s].” Trade After the creation of three annual “dialogues” on trade within the COP30 Belém “global mutirão” decision, the topic was not expected to feature on the official agenda, even if it was likely to come up in other negotiating tracks. But, in the end, the rejection of not only the cover decision, but also agreements on “response measures” and agriculture, meant that trade was entirely missing from the COP31 outcome. (See: Response measures and Agriculture .) (A request from the African group to add trade to the COP31 agenda was also rejected .) Trade and climate featured strongly in the first “ reflections ” text on a cover decision, which was a compilation of suggestions from parties. Paragraph 119 of the first draft “call[ed] on” developed countries to “phase out unilateral…trade-restrictive measures” by the end of 2027. Commonly cited examples of what this might refer to include the EU’s carbon border adjustment mechanism and deforestation law. (See: Agriculture and food security .) First draft of the COP31 cover decision. Source: UNFCCC The phase-out call was, expectedly, cut from the second iteration of the cover text.    Speaking to Carbon Brief, global policy advisor at Greenpeace East Asia Yao Zhe said: “No one thought it would survive, probably even the ones [who] proposed it. But I see it as an indication that [countries] are persistent in pushing the trade angle.” Yao added that she expected China, with the African group, to “aim for higher” on trade at next year’s COP32 summit. In the end, with the “Antalya pact” failing, none of the references to trade survived the conference. In the closing plenary, Russia, Venezuela, Brazil, Iran, Kenya – with the Arab and African groups – lamented how the issue of trade was treated in the talks, with Saudi Arabia saying developing countries were told “this is a matter that is completely off the table”. Russia’s representative remarked that “climate policy should not turn into trade policy by other means”, calling customs tariffs on “green” supply chains “old colonial distribution of labour under a new green banner.” Ghana, for the African group, pointed out “no firm treatment” of trade measures at COP31. Credit: IISD/ENB – Mike Muzurakis Ghana and Kenya both flagged the lack of “firm treatment” of trade measures and hinted that it would be a priority for them at COP32. Kenya’s delegate said: “Unilateral trade measures are only noted. African economies bear their costs, while the decision merely notes their views.”  Second global stocktake Against a backdrop of fraught negotiations, the second “ global stocktake ” (GST) was launched at a high-level event in the middle of the second week of COP31. The GST is the Paris Agreement’s five-yearly “ reality check ”, measuring whether the world’s collective efforts are enough to sufficiently cut emissions and prepare for climate impacts. The first stocktake culminated in Dubai at COP28 in 2023, resulting in the first-ever global commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels ”, among various other pledges. GST2 will run until 2028, meaning COP33 will have to address the likely shortfall between the Paris Agreement’s goals and reality. An important question hanging over this process is whether parties will have access to the latest IPCC science in time for the second GST, as a small group of countries push for the next IPCC report to be published after the stocktake. (See: Cover text. ) COP31 also featured a “dialogue” on how the lessons of the first GST could inform countries’ future NDCs.  Parties such as the EU and climate-vulnerable nations argued for a more substantial outcome that included guidance for the second GST and references to the 1.5C target. This was opposed by many developing countries. In the end, parties decided on a procedural outcome without any of the more ambitious language that had appeared in previous drafts . Long-term goal review COP31 was unable to agree on whether to start a third “periodic review” of the UN climate convention ’s long-term goal and progress towards meeting it. The goal of the 1992 convention is to avoid “dangerous” climate change, a target that was defined at COP16 in 2010 as a warming limit of 2C. COP16 also said that this goal – and progress towards meeting it – should be subject to “periodic review”. The first review , in 2013-2015, helped secure the Paris 1.5C limit. At the start of the second review at COP25 , some parties disputed the need for the process, given the existence of five-yearly “ global stocktakes ” of progress under the Paris Agreement. Underlying this disagreement is the fact that the convention has distinct country requirements for developed and developing parties, whereas the Paris regime does not. Discussions on a third review stalled at COP29 and continued at COP30. Some developed countries said it was “ redundant ”, while developing countries wanted it to continue. In Antalya, countries were split over whether to begin a third periodic review, whether to delay it until publication of the next IPCC report, or whether to discontinue the process. The final COP31 text “notes the consideration” of the matter and decides to continue talking at COP32 next year. At the first closing plenary , China, along with India for the LMDCs and Saudi Arabia for the Arab group, expressed their “concern” over the lack of agreement. China said: “We are seriously concerned that some developed country parties…in the name of streamlined process…substantively tried to terminate this mechanism.” For AOSIS, Palau “regret[ted]” the lack of progress on what it said was the “only dedicated space to reflect on the 1.5C limit on the basis of substantive scientific input”. Guidance on NDCs COP31 was unable to agree on further guidance for countries when preparing their climate pledges under the Paris Agreement, known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs). This issue has been disputed in the past, with talks also failing at COP29 in Baku two years ago. In Antalya, parties were once again split over whether to issue further guidance Developed and vulnerable countries – including the EU and small island states – want more guidance, to prompt stronger implementation and more transparent pledges. The LMDCs, the Arab group and African group, prefer to avoid what they see as prescriptive further guidance that could impinge on the “nationally determined” nature of the documents. The negotiations were subject to “ rule 16 ”, meaning they ended without agreement and will resume at the next session of the talks in Bonn next June. Rio synergies To the dismay of many countries, negotiations on the need for “synergies” between the three Rio conventions of climate change, biodiversity loss and land desertification ended with the adoption of just a one-line text .  The text simply states that, during negotiations under this item – known as “cooperation with other international organisations” – there was an “exchanges of views” and an agreement to “continue consideration at the next session”. The agreed text for the “cooperation with other international organisations” agenda item. Source: UNFCCC . On 10 November – the second day of COP – ENB reported that Russia, supported by the Arab group, “opposed continuing the discussion” on Rio synergies. Speaking on the behalf of 14 small island developing states in plenary on 14 November, Fiji said it was “deeply disappointed” by the outcome. It told delegates: “We came to Antalya ready to advance cooperation across Rio conventions and to foster synergies in national implementation. That is what all parties agreed to do when we left Bonn . We did not do that. Not because the issues were too difficult, but because we were never permitted to discuss them in the way we intended to do so. “At the very first informal consultation, before a single substantive proposal had been heard, the intention to invoke ‘ rule 16 ’ was announced by one group of party. We offered repeatedly to address any and all concerns. That offer was not taken up. Substantive discussion was blocked from the very first hour to the last.” The EIG, Panama for AILAC, the UK for the Umbrella group and the EU all expressed similar disappointment. Around the COP Fossil fuels The issue of “transitioning away from fossil fuels” dominated again at COP31, with countries leaving the talks still deeply divided on how it should be taken forward. Including “transitioning away from fossil fuels” in the cover decision was one of the key asks of a group of 126 countries spanning Europe, the small island states, parts of Latin America and the Caribbean and other major developed countries. In the end, several countries rejected the proposed cover decision over its lack of a clear reference to fossil fuels, with the EU saying: “We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” Fossil fuels also featured prominently on the sidelines at COP, with more than 80 side events and talks dedicated to the topic, Carbon Brief understands. In addition, eight European and small island nations announced intentions to release national roadmaps away from fossil fuels – bringing the total number with such plans up to 27. The first major event on fossil fuels took place on the summit’s second day, when the Brazilian COP30 presidency formally presented its global fossil-fuel roadmap to a packed-out plenary room. Another part of the text also “welcome[d]” the Brazil-led global roadmaps on the transition away from fossil fuels and on ending deforestation. The next day, a group of European and small island state ministers held a press conference on the need to transition away from fossil fuels. Denmark, Spain, Portugal and Luxembourg announced that they intend to release new national roadmaps away from fossil fuels.  (Earlier that day, Vanuatu had announced its own national roadmap and the development of a Pacific regional roadmap away from fossil fuels.)  Speaking as a united front, the group of ministers called for the language on fossil fuels contained within the first draft to be strengthened and given more prominence. However, Carbon Brief understands that, behind-the-scenes, hopes that any kind of fossil-fuel language would survive into the second draft cover decision were fast evaporating. On 18 November, a group of global-south ministers held a press conference, attended by Carbon Brief, to show their support for transitioning away from fossil fuels. At the event, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and Guatemala announced that they were joining the fossil fuel treaty , an initiative to develop a legal instrument to control fossil fuels. This brought the total number of countries supporting the treaty up to 30. During the press conference, Panama environment minister Juan Carlos Navarro made headlines with an explosive speech, telling journalists that the world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia”. The next day, the co-hosts of the second transitioning away from fossil fuels conference – Tuvalu and Ireland – held a press conference. They confirmed that a pre-conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels would be held in Dublin in May, with the actual conference taking place in Tuvalu in July. Speaking at the press conference, Tuvalu climate minister Maina Talia publicly acknowledged he was not expecting to see transitioning away from fossil fuels in the second draft of the cover decision. The co-hosts also confirmed that a third transitioning away from fossil fuels conference will be held in 2028. (Lula told civil society at COP that Brazil was keen to host it. Carbon Brief understands Cambodia and Ghana are also interested.) Later that day, a second draft cover decision was published. It did not mention “fossil fuels” at all, nor “paragraph 28 of decision 1/CMA.5”, the passage of text from the first global stocktake that calls for countries to contribute to “transitioning away from fossil fuels”. In the evening, Kurum and Bowen held a press conference to defend their second draft and tried to bat away questions from journalists about whether the removal of fossil-fuel language represented “backsliding”. Both presidents cited their push to get countries to sign up to electrification as complementary to transitioning away from fossil fuels, with Bowen telling journalists: “The world agreed at COP28 to transition away from fossil fuels. What we’re about is practical ways to do that. There’s no better way than electrification.”  However, it was widely understood that many countries were not happy with the omission of fossil fuels.
