(Source: Author research) At the national level, the DPP’s primary concern is whether it can maintain its electoral coalition after holding the presidency for three consecutive terms. Lai’s 2024 victory, with 40 percent of the popular vote, fell short of a majority. The ensuing lack of control over the legislature has rendered him unable to effectively enact his agenda. Partisan fights over the central budget, defense, and legislative power have resulted in legislative gridlock throughout much of 2025 and 2026. When coupled with the failure of a set of recall campaigns to remove KMT legislators in mid-2025, the party’s legitimacy may have suffered in the eyes of voters ( China Brief , July 7, 2025). A strong DPP showing in northern and central Taiwan would show that the party can maintain support beyond its traditional southern strongholds. Optimistic projections for the DPP describe the party as “sitting on three, looking at four, and gazing at five” (坐三望四看五) of the six special municipalities. This refers to the party having a good chance of taking Tainan, Kaohsiung, and New Taipei, an even chance of taking Taipei, and an outside chance in Taichung ( LTN , November 12). Conversely, a poor performance could reinforce perceptions of public dissatisfaction with the administration and may spell trouble for Lai’s reelection bid. The elections may help clarify the TPP’s future, too. In 2024, presidential candidate Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) received roughly 26 percent of the vote, while his party secured just over 22 percent of the party-list vote. The TPP has struggled with an identity crisis since then, however, and under the leadership of chairperson Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) has closely aligned itself with KMT legislative priorities and pursued a confrontational approach with the DPP. Its decision to cooperate with the KMT in the 2026 local elections may be a marriage of convenience where both opposition parties coordinate to improve their chances of defeating DPP candidates. A strong KMT performance could encourage the two opposition parties to pursue another joint presidential ticket in 2028, though the coalition is already fraying in some places, raising the chances that they will fail to coordinate effectively, just as happened in 2024 ( CNA , September 9). Two alternative options involve the TPP either concluding that its independent electoral base remains sufficiently large to justify fielding its own candidate, or deciding to enter a quid-pro-quo arrangement where it runs a joint ticket with the KMT in exchange for political or legislative concessions. Persistent PRC Pressure Through Interference and Transnational Repression Cross-Strait relations are not a priority issue for this election, but attempts by the People’s Republic of China (PRC) to interfere, including through ongoing acts of transnational repression, loom large over the election. Candidates have had different reasons for avoiding the issue. DPP candidates may be downplaying the issue to shake the label that the party simply campaigns on the platform of “protecting Taiwan through opposing the PRC” (抗中保台). KMT and TPP candidates, conversely, may avoid the subject because PRC electoral interference efforts often benefit their candidates. For instance, a TPP candidate for Taoyuan City councilor, Chou Hsiao-yun (周曉芸), was recently indicted for allegedly taking campaign funds from Chinese Communist Party (CCP) officials and collecting photos of Taiwanese citizens for PRC bot farms to deploy to influence electoral narratives ( SET News ; KNews , November 20; Taipei Times , November 24). PRC disinformation campaigns appear to have stepped up this year. Taiwan’s National Security Bureau recorded more than 2.5 million instances of misleading online content between January and September, compared to 1.7 million during the same period in 2025. These campaigns have targeted issues such as energy policy, food safety, defense, candidate platforms, and local infrastructure development ( TaiSounds , October 21). The PRC also seems to have escalated its transnational repression to include physical intimidation. Recent cases include an assault on comedian Huang Yi-hao (黃逸豪) that is alleged to have been directed by PRC-based instigators, a smear campaign against entertainment personality Tsai Kang-yong (蔡康永) for attending a Puma Shen rally, and an outstanding arrest warrant and cash bounty against Shen himself. These incidents remind voters that the PRC remains a factor, even in an election mainly fought over domestic priorities ( UDN , October 7; China Brief , November 5).  [3] Conclusion The results of the nine-in-one elections will predominantly reflect voter sentiment on quality-of-life issues and political personalities. They will also provide a temperature check on the Lai administration, and signal whether voters are satisfied after a decade of DPP rule. Shifting political alliances and factional politics will likely dominate the political landscape for the next two years, as parties assess the viability of their potential candidates. The results will also have significant implications for cross-Strait relations. A strong KMT performance could strengthen the party’s argument that Taiwanese voters favor a less confrontational approach to Beijing and improve the political standing of candidates advocating renewed cross-Strait dialogue. A strong DPP performance would instead lend credence to the party’s belief that Taiwanese voters are skeptical of the KMT’s more dovish approach to Beijing. [2] Political parties in Taiwan and their allies are referred to in different colors. The DPP is the Green camp (綠營) or pan-Green camp (泛綠), the KMT is the Blue camp (藍營) or pan-Blue camp (泛藍), and the TPP’s colors are white. [3] The impact of Beijing’s traditional united front activities appears more limited in scope. 摘要：在党的二十大上，以前组织部部长陈曦为中心的清华系是习近平周围的权力极之一。随着中央政治局委员陈吉宁被立案调查，清华13名正部级以上官员中，有7人被立案调查、下台或撤职。派系的崩溃是从陈汐的失宠开始的。 6月，习近平破格保留的中央党校校长职务在陈曦任期结束前由蔡奇接任。一个失宠的派系没有人为其担保，并担任其他人觊觎的职位，从而加速其崩溃。该集团的核心成员陈吉宁被空降到上海，在那里的四年里几乎没有什么表现。对人工智能的大量投资并没有取得重大突破。这使得习近平很容易将他视为五中全会全面从严治党运动的反面典型。 11月24日，新华社发布消息称，中共中央政治局委员、上海市委书记陈吉宁涉嫌严重违纪违法，目前正接受中央纪律检查委员会组织调查（新华社11月24日电）。上海市委当晚表示支持这一决定（上海市人民政府，11月24日）。
陈是继2006年陈良宇之后第四位落马的第20届政治局委员，也是第二位被落马的上海市委书记（中国网，2006年9月25日）。他曾被广泛视为2027年下半年党的第二十一次代表大会政治局常委的竞争者（华尔街日报，11月24日）。同日，原西安市委书记方红卫与陈清华一样，均是清华大学毕业生，被起诉（财新网，2021年11月7日；新华社，11月24日）。陈吉宁的事业与习近平总书记的清华同学陈希密不可分。陈曦留在了大学，并通过共青团和学生事务晋升为校党委书记。 2013年起，主持中组部日常工作，后出任中组部部长（人民网，2017年10月25日；路透社，2022年10月10日）。他以清华为基地，建立了一个高层网络，被称为“清华帮”。 [1] 2023年，本应完全退休的他却破格留任中央党校校长，从而保留了影响力（人民网，2017年10月25日；联合早报，6月5日）。但从那时起，由于一些成员受到控制或调查，该集团逐渐衰落。 6月，陈曦在任期届满前突然交出国家主席职务（《联合早报》6月5日）。
同月，据信与陈曦关系密切的北京政协主席魏小东受到调查（新华社，6 月 6 日；中国主义，6 月 8 日）。陈吉宁的倒台可能标志着清华系的终结。清华派大半出局，陈吉宁的每次升迁，都追随着陈曦的位置。陈吉宁在2006年和2007年担任清华大学副校长和常务副校长时，陈希担任清华大学党委书记。当他直接从清华大学校长那里走出来的时候

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary: At the 20th Party Congress, the Tsinghua Clique—centered on former Organization Department head Chen Xi—was one of the poles of power around Xi Jinping. With Politburo member Chen Jining now under investigation, seven of the 13 Tsinghua-affiliated officials at full ministerial rank or above have been placed under investigation, stepped down, or been moved out of their posts. The clique’s collapse began with Chen Xi’s fall from favor. In June, the Central Party School presidency, which Xi had kept for him as an exception, went to Cai Qi before Chen Xi’s term was up. A faction that has lost favor has no one to vouch for it and holds posts others covet, accelerating its collapse. Chen Jining, a core member of the clique, was parachuted into Shanghai and had little to show for his four years there. Heavy investment in artificial intelligence produced no major breakthroughs. This made it easy for Xi to discard him as a negative example for the Fifth Plenum’s campaign of full and rigorous Party self-governance. On November 24, Xinhua announced that Politburo member and Shanghai Party Secretary Chen Jining (陈吉宁) is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) for suspected serious violations of discipline and law ( Xinhua , November 24). Shanghai’s Party committee pledged its support for the decision that evening ( Shanghai Municipal Government , November 24). Chen is the fourth member of the 20th Politburo to fall, and the second Shanghai Party secretary brought down in office, after Chen Liangyu (陈良宇) in 2006 ( China.org.cn , September 25, 2006). He had been widely seen as a contender for the Politburo Standing Committee at the 21st Party Congress in the second half of 2027 ( Wall Street Journal , November 24). The same day, Fang Hongwei (方红卫), a former Party secretary of Xi’an who, like Chen, is a Tsinghua graduate, was indicted ( Caixin , November 7, 2021; Xinhua , November 24). Chen Jining’s career is inseparable from that of Chen Xi (陈希), General Secretary Xi Jinping’s classmate at Tsinghua. Chen Xi stayed on at the university and rose through the Communist Youth League and student affairs to become its Party secretary. From 2013, he ran the Central Organization Department’s day-to-day work, later becoming its head ( People’s Daily Online , October 25, 2017; Reuters , October 10, 2022). With Tsinghua as his base, he built a high-level network known as the “Tsinghua Clique” (清华帮).  [1] In 2023, when he should have fully retired, he was granted an exception to stay on as president of the Central Party School, allowing him to retain his influence ( People’s Daily Online , October 25, 2017; Lianhe Zaobao , June 5). Yet from then on the clique declined, as some of its members were reined in or investigated. In June, Chen Xi abruptly handed over the presidency before his term was up ( Lianhe Zaobao , June 5). That same month, Wei Xiaodong (魏小东), chairman of the Beijing Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC) who is believed to have close ties to Chen Xi, was placed under investigation ( Xinhua , June 6; Sinocism , June 8). Chen Jining’s fall likely marks the end of the Tsinghua Clique. Most of the Tsinghua Clique Is Out Each of Chen Jining’s promotions tracked Chen Xi’s position. When Chen Jining became vice president and then executive vice president of Tsinghua in 2006 and 2007, Chen Xi was the university’s Party secretary. When he went straight from Tsinghua president to minister of environmental protection in 2015, and when he became acting mayor of Beijing in 2017, Chen Xi was running the day-to-day work of the Organization Department. In October 2022, Chen Xi personally announced Chen Jining’s appointment as Shanghai Party secretary ( People’s Daily Online , February 27, 2015; Xinhua , October 28, 2022). Around the 20th Party Congress, Tsinghua cadres with ties to Chen Xi held posts in the Organization Department, the Central Party School, and other central bodies, as well as in Shanghai, Beijing, and several other provinces and cities. Counting only those who studied full-time or worked at Tsinghua, 13 officials held full ministerial rank or above after the 20th Party Congress.  [2] Of these, seven are now out (see Table 1). Hu Heping (胡和平) stepped down as minister of culture and tourism at the end of 2023, retaining only his deputy post at the Propaganda Department (Xinhua, December 29, 2023 , October 30 ). Former Organization Department head Li Ganjie (李干杰), a core figure in Chen Xi’s control over personnel, was transferred in April 2025 to the less influential United Front Work Department ( Central News Agency , April 2, 2025). Hubei Party Secretary Wang Menghui (王蒙徽) and Henan Party Secretary Liu Ning (刘宁) were moved to sinecures at the National People’s Congress (NPC) as they neared retirement age, and Hebei Party Secretary Ni Yuefeng (倪岳峰) followed suit well before reaching it (Xinhua, February 25, 2025 , August 28 , November 6 ). In little more than a year, Fang Hongwei, Qin Weizhong (覃伟中), Xia Linmao (夏林茂), and Chen Jining have all been placed under investigation (Xinhua, November 7, 2025 , September 21 , October 22 ). Everyone Kicks a Faction When It Is Down The two most important posts Chen Xi’s network lost have gone to others. Shi Taifeng (石泰峰), head of the Organization Department since April 2025, was one of Xi’s deputies when Xi was president of the Central Party School, and later served as governor of Jiangsu under Party Secretary—and now second-ranking Politburo Standing Committee member—Li Qiang (李强) ( Xinhua , June 11, 2017; People’s Daily Online , October 25, 2017). In June, the Central Party School presidency went to Cai Qi (蔡奇), Xi’s chief of staff ( Lianhe Zaobao , June 5; Xinhua , June 18). Once a faction’s patron loses favor, its collapse feeds on itself, for three reasons. First, no one will vouch for its members. Under a 2016 Party directive, when officials with a record of poor conduct are promoted (带病提拔), every stage of their selection is reviewed, and the organization departments and leading officials involved are held accountable ( People’s Daily Online , August 29, 2016). To speak up for a member of a fallen faction is to stake one’s own future on him. Second, faction members are now in the way. Every post they hold can go to someone else’s protégés, and those who take over have every incentive to consolidate their positions and none to defend their predecessors. Third, the investigations necessarily target the work that the fallen patron had overseen. In the case of Chen Xi, Cao Xingxin (曹兴信), Chen’s former subordinate at the Organization Department, was investigated in 2024 and punished for having “sought benefits for others in the selection and appointment of officials” (在干部选拔任用工作中为他人谋取利益) (Xinhua, September 28, 2024 , February 24, 2025 ; The Paper , September 28, 2024). As the Organization Department was Chen’s portfolio for a decade, pulling on this thread has led mostly to officials he promoted. And as each cadre has fallen, the remaining members have become more isolated and at the mercy of rivals. Table 1: Fates of Leading Tsinghua Clique Members since the 20th Party Congress Name Post after the 20th Party Congress Outcome Date Chen Xi 陈希 Head of the Organization Department; President of the Central Party School (former Politburo member; vice-national rank) Stepped down from the Organization Department, then the Central Party School April 2023; June 2026 Chen Jining 陈吉宁 Politburo member; Shanghai Party Secretary (vice-national) Under investigation November 2026 Li Ganjie 李干杰 Politburo member; head of the Organization Department from April 2023 (vice-national) Moved to head of the United Front Work Department April 2025 Hu Heping 胡和平 Minister of Culture and Tourism; deputy head of the Propaganda Department (full ministerial) Kept only the Propaganda Department post December 2023 Wang Menghui 王蒙徽 Hubei Party Secretary (full ministerial) Moved near retirement age to vice chair of the NPC Environmental Protection and Resources Conservation Committee December 2024 Liu Ning 刘宁 Guangxi Party Secretary, later Henan Party Secretary (full ministerial) Moved near retirement age to vice chair of the NPC Agriculture and Rural Affairs Committee September 2026 Ni Yuefeng 倪岳峰 Hebei Party Secretary (full ministerial) Moved before retirement age to vice chair of the NPC Social Development Affairs Committee July 2026 Wang Xiqin 王希勤 President of Tsinghua University (vice-ministerial) Moved to deputy director of the National Natural Science Foundation; later left the post for undisclosed reasons December 2023; October 2025 Fang Hongwei 方红卫 Shaanxi Party Standing Committee member; Xi’an Party Secretary (vice-ministerial) Under investigation; since indicted November 2025 Qin Weizhong 覃伟中 Shenzhen Mayor (vice-ministerial) Moved to the Party group of the Guangdong Provincial People’s Congress Standing Committee; later placed under investigation September 2026 Xia Linmao 夏林茂 Beijing Party Standing Committee member; vice mayor (vice-ministerial) Under investigation October 2026 Wang Weizhong 王伟中 Guangdong Governor (full ministerial) Promoted to Inner Mongolia Party Secretary September 2025 Yin Yong 殷勇 Beijing Mayor (full ministerial) In office — Chen Xu 陈旭 Deputy head of the United Front Work Department; director of the State Council Overseas Chinese Affairs Office (full ministerial) In office — Liu Xiaokai 刘晓凯 Guizhou CPPCC Chairman (full ministerial) Moved to Yunnan CPPCC Chairman January 2023 Gao Yunlong 高云龙 CPPCC Vice Chairman; Chairman of the All-China Federation of Industry and Commerce (vice-national) In office — Wang Guangqian 王光谦 Executive Vice Chairman of the China Democratic League; CPPCC Vice Chairman from March 2023 (vice-national) In office — (Source: Author’s compilation from official appointment announcements by Xinhua, People’s Daily Online, the NPC, and others. Besides the 13 officials at full ministerial rank or above, the table lists four vice-ministerial officials: Wang Xiqin, Fang Hongwei, Qin Weizhong, and Xia Linmao.) Chen Jining Had No Record to Shield Himself Chen Jining’s achievements lay in sectoral work. His signature accomplishment came as minister of environmental protection. By 2016, his second year in the post, PM2.5 concentrations in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei region had fallen 33 percent from 2013 levels ( People’s Daily Online , January 5, 2017). Yet after becoming Shanghai’s “number one” (一把手), he had little to show for four years at the helm. Instead, the most notable event on his watch was the protest on Urumqi Middle Road less than a month after he took office ( BBC , November 27, 2022; China Brief , December 8, 2022). Though he had little to do with it, it became the first mark on his record. Xi directed Shanghai to make building its “five centers” (五个中心) the main thrust of its work and to “take the lead” (走在前列) in artificial intelligence (AI) (Xinhua, December 3, 2023 , April 29, 2025 ). To this end, Shanghai set up a string of government- and university-branded AI research institutes, established a renminbi (RMB) 22.5 billion ($3.4 billion) AI fund of funds, and in 2025 issued RMB 1 billion ($149 million) in vouchers for computing power, models, and training data in a single round ( SSCI Leading Fund , accessed November 24; Shanghai Municipal Government , July 28, 2025). The spending has not produced convincing results. MiniMax (稀宇科技), Shanghai’s best-known large-model company, fell below its offering price less than a year after listing and is down more than 88 percent from its peak ( Caixin , October 22). Shanghai’s own auditors found that subsidies for three “high-quality incubators” sat idle, that only 33 of the 279 companies backed by an incubator-linked investment fund actually came from incubators, and that RMB 18.5 billion ($2.8 billion) in technology loans had been diverted to urban renewal ( Shanghai Municipal Government , September 20). Shanghai—a higher-ranking municipality directly under the central government—threw the whole city’s resources at AI and still did no better than Hangzhou, which relied on private companies.  [3] This likely disappointed Xi, falling short of both his ambitions and his expectations. Conclusion Chen Jining is the first Politburo member to fall since the Fifth Plenum in late October. The plenum’s Resolution states that the Party has “removed serious dangers hidden within the Party, the state, and the military” (消除了党、国家、军队内部存在的严重隐患), and traces most remaining problems to the officials at all levels who carry out policy ( China Brief , November 18). Less than a month later, accountability for implementation has come down on a Politburo member with an iron fist. Xi had singled out Shanghai to lead in AI. Chen Jining could not deliver, and no one would vouch for him over his other problems. The Resolution also calls for improving “the mechanisms for holding to account those responsible for promoting officials with a record of poor conduct” (干部“带病提拔”责任追究机制) and “firmly eliminating self-serving cliques” (坚决破除“小圈子”) ( Xinhua , November 1). The Tsinghua Clique fits that description—and has consequently lost favor. The rest of Chen Xi’s network can be expected to exit one by one around the 21st Party Congress, and accountability may yet reach Chen Xi himself. Any group that loses Xi’s trust will meet the same fate, as rivals pile on and allies scatter. Notes [1] Here, the Tsinghua Clique refers to officials centered on Chen Xi who studied full-time or worked at Tsinghua, plus his former subordinates at the Organization Department, rather than Tsinghua alumni in general. Xi himself and 20th Politburo members Li Xi (李希) (EMBA), Huang Kunming (黄坤明), and Zhang Guoqing (张国清) (both in-service doctorates) are excluded. On the system for cultivating and transferring cadres that Chen Xi built while running Tsinghua, see Wen-Hsuan Tsai and Xingmiu Liao, “The Impending Rise of the ‘Tsinghua Clique’: Cultivation, Transfer, and Relationships in Chinese Elite Politics,” Journal of Contemporary China 28, no. 120 (2019): 948–64, https://doi.org/10.1080/10670564.2019.1594106 . [2] The 13 are Chen Xi, Chen Jining, Li Ganjie, Hu Heping, Chen Xu, Wang Menghui, Ni Yuefeng, Liu Ning, Wang Weizhong, Yin Yong, Liu Xiaokai, Gao Yunlong, and Wang Guangqian. The count covers the period from the 20th Party Congress to the March 2023 leadership transition and is based on official biographies. In-service graduate degrees and EMBAs are not counted. [3] Hangzhou’s momentum in AI is clearly stronger than Shanghai’s. DeepSeek, Unitree, and the rest of the “six little dragons of Hangzhou” (杭州六小龙) all come from the city ( South China Morning Post , February 10, 2025; China Brief , March 19, 2025). According to a report by the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design, Hangzhou accounted for 16 percent of the notable AI models released worldwide over the past year and a half, the highest share of any Chinese city ( Yicai Global , November 24). The Chinese model most downloaded and most widely adapted in the global open-source community is Alibaba’s Qwen (通义千问), developed in Hangzhou ( Hugging Face , August 14). The post Fall of Politburo’s Chen Jining Marks End of Tsinghua Clique appeared first on Jamestown .

title: Hong Kong’s Police Training Advances Beijing’s Global Reach
zh_title: 香港警察培训提升北京的全球影响力
summary: 内容提要 香港新成立的警察学院为北京提供了一种通过国际公认的机构输出中国安全实践的途径。随着北京的警察机构与中华人民共和国的警察机构趋同，这座城市剩余的独特性可能对北京变得更有用。英国的学术声望可以促进香港警务转型。剑桥大学培训的导师可以为当地学位提供可信度，重现中国机构的优先事项，从而使代际变革能够在不立即与英国决裂的情况下继续进行。
content:
内容提要 香港新成立的警察学院为北京提供了一种通过国际公认的机构输出中国安全实践的途径。随着北京的警察机构与中华人民共和国的警察机构趋同，这座城市剩余的独特性可能对北京变得更有用。英国的学术声望可以促进香港警务转型。剑桥大学培训的导师可以为复制中国机构优先事项的本地学位提供可信度，从而允许代际变革在不立即打​​破英国教育传统的情况下进行。海外培训可以塑造对中国装备的需求，并培养外国安全机构内部的联系。将指导与采购和专业标准联系起来还可以将北京的影响力从个别官员扩展到受援机构的运作方式。 11月11日，香港国际警务学院揭牌，并与柬埔寨和沙特阿拉伯的警察学院签署培训协议（香港警务处，11月11日）。除了这个国际平台之外，学院还将提供专门从事安全和刑事调查的应用学位课程（香港电台 [RTHK]，10 月 9 日）。这些举措将在国内培养政治上可靠的官员与输出香港的专业声誉联系起来。
北京将获得一个培训体系，其国际身份仍明显保留香港的特色，但其机构内容越来越多地反映中国公共安全的优先事项。 学院扩展香港的警察外交 学院的目标是通过 20 多个项目和论坛，每年培训约 1,000 名警官，其中包括约 200 名海外人员（香港政府，11 月 11 日）。课程涵盖刑事调查和反恐、战术指挥和情报等更敏感的职能。只有五名官员将协调现有的培训资源（文汇报，10 月 9 日）。因此，香港可以通过汇集其警察机构内现有的专业知识来扩大其外交作用。香港警方最近与柬埔寨警察学院、澳大利亚警察管理学院、埃及警察学院和哈萨克斯坦阿拉木图学院合作（另类，2025年12月17日；香港警务处，11月13日访问）。这些关系的范围从交流到培训外国教练。香港于2026年3月培训柬埔寨战术教官，并与荷兰、泰国、新加坡和越南进行交流（另类，2025年6月11日；4月15日；大公报，5月23日）。将这些联系纳入一个共同机构可以使香港成为海外官员专业发展的经常参考点。
领导人论坛将针对东南亚、中东和其他“一带一路”合作伙伴（香港警务处，11月11日）。香港即将主办国际刑事警察组织（国际刑警组织）大会，香港海关担任世界海关组织亚太区副主席，为推动“一国两制”提供平台（文汇报，10月9日；香港海关，10月） 15）。这一框架利用香港的国际地位来支持这样的说法，即香港保留着独特的、与全球相连的地位。

【原文 English Original】
Executive Summary Hong Kong’s new police academy offers Beijing a way to export Chinese security practices through an internationally recognizable institution. The city’s remaining distinctiveness may become more useful to Beijing as its police institutions converge with those of the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC). British academic prestige can facilitate Hong Kong’s policing transition. Cambridge University-trained supervisors can lend credibility to a local degree that reproduces Chinese institutional priorities, allowing generational change to proceed without an immediate break with British educational traditions. Overseas training can shape demand for Chinese equipment and cultivate contacts inside foreign security institutions. Linking instruction to procurement and professional standards also could extend Beijing’s influence beyond individual officers into how recipient agencies operate. On November 11, Hong Kong inaugurated its International Academy of Policing and signed training agreements with police academies in Cambodia and Saudi Arabia ( Hong Kong Police Force , November 11). Alongside this international platform, the academy will offer an applied degree program specializing in security and criminal investigations ( Radio Television Hong Kong [RTHK] , October 9). These initiatives link the cultivation of politically reliable officers at home with the export of Hong Kong’s professional reputation. Beijing stands to gain a training system whose international identity remains recognizably Hong Kong’s but whose institutional content increasingly reflects Chinese public security priorities. The Academy Extends Hong Kong’s Police Diplomacy The academy aims to train approximately 1,000 officers annually, including around 200 overseas personnel, through more than 20 programs and forums ( Hong Kong Government , November 11). Courses span criminal investigation and more sensitive functions such as counterterrorism, tactical command, and intelligence. Just five officers will coordinate existing training resources ( Wen Wei Po , October 9). Hong Kong can therefore expand its diplomatic role by pooling expertise already available within its police institutions. Hong Kong’s police have recently worked with Cambodia’s Police Academy, the Australian Institute of Police Management, Egypt’s Police Academy, and Kazakhstan’s Almaty Academy ( Offbeat , December 17, 2025; Hong Kong Police Force , accessed November 13). These relationships range from exchanges to training foreign instructors. Hong Kong trained Cambodian tactical instructors in March 2026, and held exchanges with the Netherlands, Thailand, Singapore, and Vietnam (Offbeat, June 11, 2025 ; April 15 ; Ta Kung Pao , May 23). Bringing these contacts into a common institution can make Hong Kong a recurring reference point in overseas officers’ professional development. Leadership forums will target Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, and other One Belt One Road (OBOR) partners ( Hong Kong Police Force , November 11). Hong Kong’s forthcoming hosting of the International Criminal Police Organization (INTERPOL) General Assembly and its Customs service’s Asia-Pacific vice-chairmanship of the World Customs Organization offer platforms for promoting “one country, two systems” (一國兩制) ( Wen Wei Po , October 9; Hong Kong Customs and Excise Department , October 15). This framing uses Hong Kong’s international standing to support the claim that the city retains a distinct and globally connected role under Chinese sovereignty. Participation in the Association of Police Training Institutions in Asia and Dubai’s international policing best-practice conference provides established channels (Offbeat, April 22, 2015 , December 23, 2020 ). These forums could give Hong Kong a wider role in defining the terms of international police cooperation. Training Can Export an Integrated Policing System Hong Kong offers Beijing an intermediary whose international credibility partly rests on relationships predating its convergence with the People’s Republic of China’s (PRC) public security system. Foreign agencies may find cooperation with Hong Kong easier to justify than direct engagement with Chinese public security authorities. Expertise acquired through international partnerships can be adapted to Chinese priorities and circulated under a familiar institutional identity. Hong Kong’s distinctiveness can thus lower the political barriers to accepting Chinese policing practices. This advantage depends on partners continuing to treat Hong Kong’s police as institutionally distinct. The potential export is an integrated system of operations, equipment, organization, and training. Teaching officers how to identify threats and organize a response also shapes which capabilities they consider necessary. If these methods become routine, Chinese influence can persist beyond the course itself, embedded in everyday institutional decisions. A regular role in multilateral training, potentially through INTERPOL-related cooperation, could also confer authority over professional standards. Selecting which threats deserve attention and which responses count as best practice can give Chinese security assumptions the status of technical expertise. Recipient agencies could absorb those assumptions through professional learning without making an explicit political commitment to Beijing. Training also offers access to foreign officers’ institutional priorities, procedures, and vulnerabilities, creating opportunities for intelligence collection and cultivation. Alumni networks could serve united-front objectives by sustaining contacts inside overseas security establishments. These remain potential uses of the relationships, not demonstrated activities of the academy. Where security-sector reform connects policing with border management, intelligence, disaster response, or military organizations, shared personnel and practices could carry that influence into the wider security apparatus. Police Education Cultivates Political Reliability At home, the degree conferred by the training program opens a door for integration within Hong Kong’s political elite. Full police funding gives serving officers without a first degree an incentive to participate ( RTHK , October 9). This builds on a model pioneered by Tsinghua University, which launched its Executive Master of Public Administration program for Hong Kong governance professionals in 2018. Alumni reported in May 2025 included constitutional affairs official Clement Woo (胡健民), the chief executive’s special assistant Jenny Wong (黃芷淵), and legislators Carmen Kan (簡慧敏), Shang Hailong (尚海龍), Edward Leung (梁熙), and Gary Zhang (張欣宇) ( Ta Kung Pao , May 17, 2025). It also builds on a separate Police College partnership, formalized in 2021, which was renewed in 2023 for three further cohorts ( Offbeat , May 24, 2023). The new degree program emerges during a period in which Hong Kong’s police force is already undergoing practical and symbolic convergence with the PRC. Chinese-style foot drills became standard in 2022 ( Deutsche Welle , January 14, 2022). Earlier revisions to its published history removed or softened references to the 1989 pro-democracy movement and the 1967 riots ( Radio France Internationale , July 19, 2016). A phased replacement program introduced Chinese-made CF98-A and CS/LP5 pistols from 2024. By May 2026, police had also confirmed adoption of CS/LS7 submachine guns by the Counter Terrorism Response Unit and Airport Security Unit ( Xinhua , November 18, 2024; China News Service , May 7). Academic credentials follow these means of institutionalizing the transition. Political education and technological familiarization already form part of professional training. The People’s Public Security University of China has hosted Hong Kong police study programs since 2001 ( People’s Public Security University of China , May 18, 2011). Partnerships also include Shanghai Police College and Guangdong Police College. A January 2024 agreement with the PRC Ministry of Public Security expanded the “6+2” training framework to “6+2+N,” which included six study programs at police institutions, two exchange programs for police tactical instructors, and multiple programs on the PRC’s national affairs. A 2023 university study program combined police developments with teaching on the Chinese Communist Party’s (CCP) 20th National Congress and a visit to Huawei’s Beijing research institute (Offbeat, August 16, 2023 ; January 8, 2025 ). A Hong Kong police alumni association for the People’s Public Security University of China was established in 2006, and the university’s then-president, Wang Yanji (王彦吉), attended its inauguration ( Offbeat , November 22, 2006). In November 2024, two superintendents and three Police College staff joined national affairs training organized by Renmin University and Beijing’s Liaison Office in Hong Kong ( Offbeat , January 22, 2025). The inclusion of teaching staff extends the reach of exchanges, because their experience can shape the curriculum for subsequent cohorts. Hong Kong’s very firstfive-year plan (2026–2030), unveiled in September 2026, explicitly connects regular training cooperation with institutions in the PRC to strengthening civil servants’ patriotic commitment ( Hong Kong Government , September 16). The new degree can give that objective a continuing institutional form. British Credentials Can Ease Institutional Change What sets Hong Kong’s police degree apart from other programs is its supervisory arrangement. Final projects are to be supervised by officers of superintendent rank or above with qualifications from Tsinghua or Cambridge University in the United Kingdom, building authority through academic pedigree ( RTHK , October 9). Hong Kong’s collaboration with Cambridge on the Master of Studies in Applied Criminology and Police Management began in 2017. Senior officers completed the course, and Cambridge academics traveled to Hong Kong for dissertation presentations and alumni exchanges ( Offbeat , December 18, 2019). These relationships supplied expertise and an internationally recognizable mark of professional status that remains available to officers trained under the earlier arrangement. Cambridge still advertises its police executive master’s program, despite the United Kingdom suspending military training for Hong Kong police in 2020 ( The Observer , August 15, 2020; University of Cambridge , accessed November 13). Hong Kong police sponsorship arrangements remain unclear, as a supervisor’s Cambridge qualification does not imply Cambridge oversight of the new degree. This gives British academic prestige a new political use: British-trained officers can validate a locally controlled degree whose graduates enter an institution increasingly shaped by Chinese priorities. As British institutional influence gradually recedes, Hong Kong is trying to establish its own prestigious academic institutions. Creating local degrees that offer sufficient recognition and career opportunities would weaken demand for overseas study, reducing the political cost of changing the force’s educational orientation. Under “patriots administering Hong Kong” (愛國者治港), familiarity with the PRC’s governance and Hong Kong’s circumstances (知國情、懂港情) may increasingly function as an informal credential for political office ( Wen Wei Po , January 24, 2021). The degree could give that political expectation a routine place in police career development. Training Connects Officers to Chinese Suppliers The 2026 Global Public Security Cooperation Forum in Lianyungang combined an equipment exhibition with initiatives on public security standardization and international police education ( Xinhua , September 9). Local authorities promoted exports of Chinese security technologies, equipment, and integrated systems through the city’s security-industry platform ( Lianyungang Fabu , September 9). Bringing training and suppliers into the same cooperation agenda can help Chinese products become familiar answers to the operational problems foreign officers are taught to address. Hong Kong’s police academy already provides a concrete connection. On November 4, Offbeat , the force’s official journal, reported that its Advanced Tactics Application Course would include visits to firearms and ammunition factories in the PRC ( Offbeat , November 4). Such visits make suppliers part of professional instruction. If agencies adopt the associated equipment and routines, maintenance, software, and retraining costs can make switching systems harder, locking the force in to dependence on PRC supply chains. Where suppliers and technologies serve both policing and defense, these relationships could also support military–civil fusion. Communications, surveillance, and border management provide plausible points of overlap. Procurement choices originating in police training could spread through shared personnel, equipment, and operating practices, connecting a wider range of security institutions to Chinese supply chains. Conclusion Under Hong Kong’s diminishing autonomy, its police force seeks to retain a British-derived professional identity while Chinese institutions increasingly shape how officers are trained and equipped. This combination uses credibility accumulated under an earlier political order to advance Chinese security priorities. Abroad, it offers a way to embed Chinese practices in institutions that might resist an overt partnership with PRC institutions. Its new International Academy of Policing could turn the distinction promised by “one country, two systems” into a means of extending one system’s influence overseas. This is part of a series examining the central importance of critical minerals and the race to ensure Western supply. Multiple US government agencies released a series of funding vehicles and new policies in August as part of efforts to build a reliable, non-Chinese, critical minerals supply chain for defense production. The announcements received relatively little fanfare outside the trade and business media, yet their ambitious goal is to reshape global supply chains. China has spent decades developing an industrial ecosystem “from soup to nuts” controlled by the Communist Party. It built an integrated natural resource supply chain, financing system, production industry, trained labor force, and large domestic market as it pursued modernization and national security. The US and Europe now see China’s dominance in critical minerals as a Western national security vulnerability . Without the minerals and rare earths China supplies, modern defense technology cannot be made at scale in the near term. To address this immediate threat, US President Donald Trump announced $3bn for mining and processing projects in August, while his administration also moved to secure supply from allied producers abroad. In March, the Pentagon had already signed a binding letter of intent to buy about $96m of light and heavy rare earth oxides from Australia’s Lynas Rare Earths over four years, redirecting funds originally earmarked for a processing facility in Texas. That month, Lynas produced the first samarium oxide at its Malaysian plant, which it says is the only commercial producer of separated samarium, terbium and dysprosium outside China. In parallel, the Pentagon is investing in domestic processing capacity, including through a 2025 loan of $150m to expand heavy rare earth separation at MP Materials’ Mountain Pass facility in California. The US cannot replicate China’s integrated critical-minerals industrial ecosystem within the timeframe required by its defense industry, and deals like these are key to protecting critical supply chains from Chinese economic coercion. Samarium is a good example. It is primarily used in samarium-cobalt (SmCo) permanent magnets, which can withstand very high temperatures and are essential in advanced technologies , such as Patriot missiles and F-35 fighter jets. Patriots are vital for missile interception, while 14 NATO allies rely on F-35 jets as a cornerstone of their modern combat air fleets. It is critical that the US and Europe work together to secure the basic supply chain that powers these integrated defense systems. In 2025, the overwhelming majority of samarium used in US production was imported from China. That year, China imposed export licensing schemes on samarium, other processed critical minerals, rare earths, and specialized processing technology, giving Beijing discretion over supply. Mines take 5-10 years to become fully productive, while processing facilities can take up to 15 years to make reliable defense-grade products. The accumulated workforce expertise required to master this complex, precise processing can take even longer to develop. Rare earth concentrate from mines like Mt. Weld in Western Australia, the source of Lynas’ samarium, is several processing stages away from magnet-grade material. Two leading American processing projects, MP Materials in California and Energy Fuels in Utah, are not expected to reach their planned expanded heavy rare earth production until 2028 or later. If China cuts off samarium, US defense output, along with allied production, would be at risk once stockpiles ran down. building resilience in the face of potential market manipulation. USA Rare Earth, another recipient of US government investment, has acquired a samarium production chain which relies on a British factory and a French stockpile with enough supply for between one and three years of US defense industry consumption. These types of industrial partnerships with Europe can fill American critical gaps. What Europe lacks in scale and investment, it makes up for in specialized expertise which is difficult, expensive, and time-consuming to replicate. Solvay, USA Rare Earth’s partner, has both a stockpile and rare-earth know-how. Its plant at La Rochelle, France, has been processing rare earths since 1948. Less Common Metals, a British metal and alloy producer, is now owned by USA Rare Earth and has a proprietary SmCo magnet production process that rivals China’s. Other German, Finnish, Swedish, and Estonian firms also have current or planned capacities across the rare earth permanent magnet supply chain—ranging from upstream mining and separation to SmCo magnet production. The European Union’s vast market offers a strong demand base for the expanding Western critical minerals production. Since adopting the Critical Raw Materials Act in 2024, the bloc has built a regulatory and policy framework for both internal investment and multilateral cooperation. The European Commission plans to establish a European Critical Raw Materials Center, designed to coordinate demand aggregation and project financing for minerals by drawing on some of the continent’s comparative strengths: market intelligence and cross-country coordination. The Center could provide a critical channel for information sharing and stakeholder mapping for US firms. This year, Washington and Brussels agreed to discuss border-adjusted price floors and offtake agreements. In addition, there are national initiatives; German companies, including BMW and Rheinmetall, said on November 23 that they planned a trading house to secure critical minerals. Europe is also widening its supplier base, and two partnerships stand out. The EU and Canada are pursuing multiple streams for critical mineral industry partnership, including closer cooperation on stockpiling and batteries, while in the longer run, the bloc’s relationship with Ukraine offers downstream demand. In July, the EU launched a defense industrial partnership with Kyiv covering drones, missile defense, artillery and other key components. Ukraine, which already mines titanium ore, has a critical minerals strategy and action plan and is actively seeking partners. No individual country has the scale or financing capability to build a fully self-reliant minerals supply chain to offset potential Chinese market manipulation. And time is short: China already dominates and has shown it is willing to restrict supplies, as it did to Japan in 2010 and to the US in 2025 , and has undercut competitors on price. Twelve NATO allies took an important step at this year’s NATO Ankara summit by formally launching a joint defense-critical raw materials initiative. The US, which is not a participant, should embrace this initiative and work with its allies to complement strategic reserves with long-term purchasing commitments and coordinated industrial investment. The immediate challenge is not to eliminate every dependency on China, but to ensure Beijing cannot interrupt essential Western defense production. The US should embrace Europe’s existing critical minerals capabilities as strategic assets, not simply temporary substitutes until American production comes online. Partnership on critical mineral supply chains both increases transatlantic security and serves as a nexus of transatlantic market growth and expertise-sharing that could move from catch-up to innovation and true resiliency. The goal should be to build a competitive allied industrial ecosystem that China cannot easily disrupt. Sharon Hudson-Dean is a Senior Fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA) and an Associate Fellow at Chatham House in London. She is a veteran diplomat and senior foreign policy leader who has managed complex strategic, defense, and political policies throughout her career. Most recently, she served as US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Northern Europe, NATO, and Arctic Security (2024-25). Anping Zhu is a Yale University student majoring in global affairs, economics, and mathematics. He is a research assistant to CEPA Fellow Sharon Hudson-Dean for her expert comment series on critical minerals and the race to secure Western supply. He is a member of the Yale Foreign Policy Initiative and has worked as a policy research intern and adviser to the governments of Lesotho and Rwanda. 美国贸易代表办公室就与制造业结构性产能过剩和生产相关的 14 项 301 条款调查做出决定并建议采取行动 2026 年 11 月 25 日星期三 - 06:19 华盛顿 — 今天，美国贸易代表杰米森·格里尔 (Jamieson Greer) 根据 1974 年《贸易法》第 301 条确定 14 个经济体与结构性过剩产能和生产相关的行为、政策和做法制造业的过剩产能和生产是不合理的，会给美国商业带来负担或限制，因此可以根据《贸易法》第 301(b) 条提起诉讼。美国贸易代表办公室（USTR）也发布了支持这些决定的具体经济报告。今天的决定涵盖的 14 个经济体是中国、欧盟、新加坡、瑞士、印度尼西亚、马来西亚、柬埔寨、泰国、韩国、越南、台湾、孟加拉国、日本和印度。贸易代表目前尚未就墨西哥或挪威做出决定。格里尔大使表示：“几十年来，我们的许多贸易伙伴采取了针对制造业、工资和劳动力抑制、金融和其他支持、非市场经济投入以及其他市场扭曲做法的产业战略，这些做法使贸易平衡向有利于他们的方向倾斜，同时侵蚀了美国的制造业基础。”
“认识到这一点，自2016年以来，从唐纳德·特朗普、乔·拜登、习近平到埃马纽埃尔·马克龙等领导人都认识到结构性产能和生产过剩对全球经济构成的威胁。但是，在七国集团、二十国集团、世贸组织和其他论坛上的连续声明没有带来变化的情况下，特朗普总统提议采取行动，消除这些不公平的行为、政策和做法。通过这样做，我们可以为美国工人创造公平的竞争环境，并制定一个新的、更世界经济的可持续发展之路。”  对于以下 14 个经济体，美国贸易代表已确定某些造成、维持或导致结构性产能和生产过剩的行为、政策和做法是不合理的，会给美国商业带来负担或限制。孟加拉国：孟加拉国的不合理行为、政策和做法包括（1）维持和扩大其制造业，特别是关键部门的工业计划； (2) 生产激励措施，促进生产和出口； （三）劳动保护不完善的； （4）金融抑制政策； (5) 未能解决全球产能和生产过剩问题，包括通过来自非市场经济体的进口和外国直接投资。这些法案、政策和做法通过以下方式给美国商业带来负担或限制：(1) 减少美国生产商和出口商在孟加拉国和第三国市场的商业机会； （二）损害美国利益
导致美国制造业的生产、出口、就业和投资损失； (3) 增加美国经济安全风险，包括对 NME 投入的依赖。在成衣和服装领域尤其如此。请在此处阅读美国贸易代表办公室的报告。柬埔寨：柬埔寨的不合理行为、政策和做法包括（1）产业政策规定了明确的出口和制造目标，而不是基于市场原则； (2) 吸收或扩大外国制造能力，特别是非市场经济国家制造能力的投资激励措施； （三）全球产能过剩问题未能解决

USTR Makes Determinations and Proposes Actions in 14 Section 301 Investigations Relating to Structural Excess Capacity and Production in Manufacturing Sectors myarbrough Wed, 11/25/2026 - 06:19 WASHINGTON – Today, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer determined under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 that the acts, policies, and practices of 14 economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has also published economy-specific reports that support the determinations. The 14 economies covered by today’s determinations are China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India. The Trade Representative has not made determinations with respect to Mexico or Norway at this time.  “For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” said Ambassador Greer . “In recognition of this, since 2016, leaders ranging from Donald Trump, to Joe Biden, to Xi Jinping, to Emmanuel Macron have recognized the threat that structural excess capacity and production poses for the global economy. But where successive statements at the G7, G20, WTO and other fora have not resulted in change, President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices. In doing so, we can level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.”  For the following 14 economies, the U.S. Trade Representative has determined that certain acts, policies, and practices which create, sustain, or contribute to structural excess capacity and production are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Bangladesh: Bangladesh’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to maintain and expand its manufacturing sector, particularly in key sectors; (2) production incentives to promote production and exports; (3) inadequate labor protections; (4) financial repression policies; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Bangladesh and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the ready-made garment and apparel sector. Read USTR’s Report here . Cambodia: Cambodia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial policies providing explicit export and manufacturing targets not based on market principles; (2) investment incentives to absorb or expand foreign manufacturing capacity, particularly from non-market economy countries; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; and (4) inadequate labor protections. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Cambodia and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like apparel, solar, and tires. Read USTR’s Report here . China: China’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) long-standing industrial plans and targeting; (2) extensive financial and other support to manufacturers; (3) support to state-owned enterprises on non-commercial terms; (4) extensive forced technology transfer; (5) wide-spread intellectual property theft; (6) inadequate labor protections, including the use of forced labor; (7) lax environmental enforcement; (8) financial repression and currency practices; and (9) encouraging the expansion of capacity and production in third countries. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in China and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in U.S. manufacturing, and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks. This is especially true in the aluminum, automotive, battery, chemical, consumer electronics, glass, machine tool, medical devices, non-ferrous metals, paper, plastics, power equipment, rail, robotics, semiconductors, ship, solar, steel, telecommunications, textiles, tires, and wind sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . European Union: The European Union’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to expand manufacturing; (2) policies to promote production and exports with high volumes of export credit; (3) sustained market access barriers; (4) preferential lending through centralized investment banks that target specific manufacturing sectors; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters to compete in the European Union and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals.   Read USTR’s Report here . India: India’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans to expand manufacturing; (2) inadequate labor protections; (3) financial repression policies; (4) sustained market access barriers; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in India and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like health (pharmaceuticals and medical devices), steel, solar, and information and communications technology (ICT).  Read USTR’s Report here . Indonesia: Indonesia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) government industrial policies to promote production and export; (2) inadequate labor laws, conditions, and enforcement; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; (4) financial repression; and (5) sector-specific acts, policies, and practices, such as “downstreaming”. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Indonesia and third country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like textiles and apparel, mining and metals production, and renewable energy. Read USTR’s Report here . Japan: Japan’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans and strategies; (2) financial repression; (3) household investment promotion; (4) support for unprofitable firms; (5) inadequate labor protections; (6) financial support for the auto, steel, semiconductor, and optical fiber industries; and (7) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Japan and third-country markets, (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector, and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, steel, semiconductors, and optical fiber. Read USTR’s Report here . Republic of Korea: Korea’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and sectoral plans to maintain and expand manufacturing; (2) preferential lending through state-owned banks; and (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Korea and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like automotive, semiconductor, and petrochemicals.  Read USTR’s Report here . Malaysia: Malaysia’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and sectoral plans to promote production and exports; (2) preferential capital through national funding vehicles that target manufacturing; (3) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies; and (4) inadequate labor protections. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Malaysia and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like information and communication technology and automotive. Read USTR’s Report here . Singapore: Singapore’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial plans; (2) financial repression; (3) savings promotion policies that suppress domestic consumption; (4) inadequate labor protections; (5) financial support for key sectors; and (6) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Singapore and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like electronics and semiconductors, health, and petrochemicals. Read USTR’s Report here . Switzerland: Switzerland’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) suppressing the appreciation of its currency below the level that would otherwise prevail under market conditions; (2) supporting its pharmaceutical sector via extensive public investment and fiscal incentives; (3) reducing a major production cost—electricity—for its steel producers; and (4) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Switzerland and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in U.S. manufacturing; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the pharmaceutical, steel, and chemicals sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . Taiwan: Taiwan’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) the recurring use of industrial and economic plans to support the manufacturing sector, particularly high-technology manufacturing; (2) legislation that incentivizes and provides support for the architecture of its industrial ecosystem; (3) state-directed and supported research and development; (4) state-directed and industrial clustering to support industry; (5) various financing mechanisms to support industry; (6) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports from non-market economies; (7) practices that equate to financial repression; (8) past purchases of U.S.-sanctioned Russian feedstock; and (9) inadequate protection of labor rights. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Taiwan and third country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like the electronics, semiconductor, and telecommunications sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . Thailand: Thailand’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) industrial and economic plans that target manufacturing and export; (2) sustained market access barriers; (3) preferential lending and other government support to industry; (4) inadequate labor protections; and (5) failure to address global excess capacity and production, including through imports and foreign direct investment from non-market economies. These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Thailand and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on NME inputs. This is especially true in the electronics, automobile, machinery, and electrical equipment sectors. Read USTR’s Report here . Vietnam: Vietnam’s unreasonable acts, policies, and practices include (1) government industrial plans and its state planning system; (2) its land planning system; (3) inadequate labor laws, conditions, and enforcement; (4) financial repression; (5) allocation of financial capital to priority sectors; (6) price regulation; (7) encouragement of or failure to address foreign direct investment from other non-market economies; (8) encouragement of or failure to address imports from other non-market economies; (9) encouragement of or failure to address transshipment from other non-market economies; and (10) sector-specific acts, policies, and practices.  These acts, policies, and practices burden or restrict U.S. commerce by (1) reducing commercial opportunities for U.S. producers and exporters in Vietnam and third-country markets; (2) harming the U.S. economy by contributing to lost production, exports, jobs, and investment in the U.S. manufacturing sector; and (3) increasing U.S. economic security risks, including through reliance on other NME inputs. This is especially true in sectors like textiles, apparel, and footwear; shipbuilding; cement; and information and communications technology. Read USTR’s Report here . As a result of these determinations, the U.S. Trade Representative has proposed responsive action in each investigation for public comment. Specifically, the U.S. Trade Representative has proposed additional tariffs on the following investigated economies except for certain products identified in the annexes of the respective Federal Register notices. Bangladesh: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Bangladesh of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Bangladesh on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States of American and the People’s Republic of Bangladesh on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Cambodia: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Cambodia of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Cambodia on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States and Cambodia on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . China: The Trade Representative proposes appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 20 percent, net of the rate of duty applied to the good under the Section 301 investigation related to the prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor, on goods of China not identified in the annexes to the relevant Federal Register notice and up to 10 percent tariffs on goods identified in Annex A to the Federal Register notice with exemptions for certain goods identified in Annex B to the Federal Register notice. The products in Annex B are products on the U.S. Imports List of the U.S.-China Board of Trade “30-For-30” Lists of Products Recommended for Reduced Tariff Treatment. This proposal accounts for the commitments and 20 percent tariff rate announced as part of the Kuala Lumpur Joint Arrangement reached by President Trump and President Xi on October 30, 2025. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . European Union: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying on all goods of the EU a tariff rate of 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with the EU on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the United States-European Union Framework Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . India: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices would include applying tariffs of up to 25 percent on all goods of India, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider whether the additional duties applied should be adjusted to account for, among others, duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions, or were India to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of India, a tariff rate of 17 percent.  Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Indonesia: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Indonesia of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Indonesia on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States and Indonesia on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Japan: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying on all goods of Japan tariffs of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain products. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Japan on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the framework agreement between the United States and Japan. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Republic of Korea: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Korea of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Korea on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Korea Strategic Trade and Investment Deal. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Malaysia: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Malaysia of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Malaysia on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Agreement between the United States and Malaysia on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Singapore: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 20 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on all goods of Singapore, with exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider adjusting the tariff rate applied to each good to 10 percent to account for any commitments in the event that Singapore were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States, or conclude other negotiations that are responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of Singapore. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Switzerland: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices proposes to consider applying on all goods of Switzerland tariffs of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Switzerland on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in United States-Switzerland-Liechtenstein Framework Agreement on Reciprocal, Fair, and Balanced Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Taiwan: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Taiwan of up to 15 percent, net of MFN rates and existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain products. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Taiwan on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the U.S.- Taiwan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Thailand: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs on all goods of Thailand of up to 18 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods. This proposal accounts for duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; ongoing consultations with Thailand on matters at issue in these investigations; and commitments relevant to certain acts, policies, and practices addressed in the Framework for an Agreement between the United States and Thailand on Reciprocal Trade. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . Vietnam: The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices includes to consider applying tariffs of up to 35 percent, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, on all goods of Vietnam, with exemptions for certain goods. The Trade Representative further proposes to consider whether the additional duties applied should be adjusted to account for, among others, duties applied under other, existing Section 301 actions; duties applied under other, existing Section 232 actions; or the commitments and a tariff rate of 20 percent, were Vietnam to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of Vietnam. Read the pre-publication version of the Federal Register notice here . To be assured of consideration, interested persons should submit requests to appear at the hearings, along with a summary of testimony by January 5, 2027 . Written comments are due by January 5, 2027 . USTR will hold hearings about the proposed actions in these investigations on January 25, 2027 , continuing as appropriate. Background: Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, as amended (Trade Act), is designed to address unfair foreign practices affecting U.S. commerce. Section 301 may be used to respond to unjustifiable, unreasonable, or discriminatory foreign government practices that burden or restrict U.S. commerce. Under Section 302(b) of the Trade Act, the United States Trade Representative may self-initiate an investigation under Section 301. On March 11, 2026, the United States Trade Representative initiated investigations into the acts, policies, and practices of various economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors. The 16 economies subject to these investigations are: China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan, and India. Pursuant to Section 304(b)(1)(A) of the Trade Act, USTR provided the public and interested persons with opportunities to present their views through a public comment process and through a public hearing. USTR received testimony of nearly 140 witnesses and 1,070 comments in response to the initiation notice and pertaining to all 16 investigated economies. Today, the U.S. Trade Representative determined, in each of 14 investigations, that the acts, policies, and practices of China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce, and are thus actionable under Section 301(b) of the Trade Act. ###
