Stratum AI 表示，在采矿业采用人工智能 (AI) 方面，它已经达到了一个“重要里程碑”——其模型支持了公开报告的矿产资源估算 (MRE)，这是采矿业首批此类案例之一。这家总部位于多伦多的深度科技公司与 St Barbara (ASX: SBM) 合作，将 Stratum 的风化和材料类型深度学习模型纳入巴布亚新几内亚 Simberi 黄金项目的 MRE 中。 Stratum 联合创始人兼首席执行官 Farzi Yusufali 表示：“St Barbara 利用 Stratum AI 的专有算法对以前被认为不适合 Simberi 现有碳浸出循环的某些矿石进行分类。” “最初的人工智能试点已经发展成为一项技术，现在支撑着 Simberi 可行性研究中的矿产资源估算。”该公司表示，MRE 的报告符合 JORC 准则，符合澳大利亚证券交易所的上市准则。人工智能在1969年勘探者放弃的地方开采铜金 Simberi位于巴布亚新几内亚的新爱尔兰省，由St Barbara、Lingbao Gold（SEHK：3330）和Kumul Mineral Holdings共同拥有。 9月，圣芭芭拉宣布有意将其在Simberi的权益出售给灵宝。该交易预计将于 2027 年初完成。Approach Stratum 已与 St Barbara 在 Simberi 合作四年多，开发基于人工智能的矿化分类方法。
这些模型最初部署在试点项目中，用于分析勘探数据。后来，它们被用于分析运营数据，使 St Barbara 能够确定哪些矿石适合通过现有的碳浸出 (CIL) 工厂进行加工，哪些矿石需要与硫化矿石一起储存以供日后处理。 Stratum 表示，能够区分矿石类型使 St Barbara 能够降低与产生额外废物相关的成本，并减少磨机的磨损。模型经过测试后，圣芭芭拉采用它们作为材料类型分类的首选方法。该模型帮助构建了 Simberi 的 2024 年资源和储量更新及其 2025 年可行性研究。 2024 年 5 月，该矿业公司表示，它在 Simberi 发现了额外 143,000 盎司的可处理材料，将矿山的处理寿命延长了 17 个月。 St Barbara 还表示，Stratum 的模型帮助其探明和推定矿石储量增加了 40%。

【原文 English Original】
Stratum AI says it has reached a “significant milestone” in the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in mining — its model has underpinned a publicly reported mineral resource estimate (MRE) in one of the first cases of its kind in the mining industry. The Toronto-based deep-tech company collaborated with St Barbara (ASX: SBM) to incorporate Stratum’s deep-learning models of weathering and material type into the MRE for the Simberi gold project in Papua New Guinea. “St Barbara has harnessed Stratum AI’s proprietary algorithms to classify certain ores that were previously considered to be unsuitable for Simberi’s existing carbon-in-leach circuit,” said Farzi Yusufali, Stratum’s co-founder and CEO. “What began as an AI pilot has evolved into a technology that now underpins the mineral resource estimate in Simberi’s feasibility study.” The company says the MRE was reported in line with the JORC Code, meeting the listing guidelines of the Australian Securities Exchange. AI strikes copper-gold where explorers gave up in 1969 Located in the province of New Ireland in Papua New Guinea, Simberi is jointly owned by St Barbara, Lingbao Gold (SEHK: 3330) and Kumul Mineral Holdings. In September, St Barbara announced its intention to sell its interest in Simberi to Lingbao. The transaction is expected to be completed in early 2027. Approach Stratum has been working with St Barbara for more than four years at Simberi to develop an AI-based approach to classify mineralization. The models were initially deployed in pilot programs to analyze exploration data. They were later used to analyze operational data, allowing St Barbara to determine which ores were suitable for processing through the existing carbon-in-leach (CIL) plant and which needed to be stockpiled for later treatment alongside sulfide ores. Stratum says being able to differentiate between ores types allowed St Barbara to reduce costs associated with generating extra waste, and saved wear and tear on the mill. After the models were tested, St Barbara adopted them as its preferred method for material-type classification. The modelling helped build Simberi’s 2024 resource and reserve update and its 2025 feasibility study. In May 2024, the mining company said it was able to identify an additional 143,000 ounces of treatable material at Simberi, extending the mine’s processing life by 17 months. St Barbara also said that Stratum’s modelling had helped increase its proved and probable ore reserves by 40%.

content: 人们对人工智能回报和针对美国贸易伙伴的新关税的担忧日益增加。(路透社：布伦丹·麦克德米德) 纳斯达克在早盘交易中下跌约 4%，市场对债务驱动的 AI 热潮能否带来足够回报的疑虑日益增加。 随着民主党在美国中期选举中获胜，该行业面临更严格的监管审查的担忧，给华尔街这个动荡月份增添了压力。 “年底反弹的基本支撑根本不存在，”西南银行首席投资官克里斯·布里加蒂在一封备忘录中说。 “受 AI 驱动的反弹正在失去动力，如果没有证据证明巨额资本支出将实现市场预期的利润和收入目标，就没有反弹的动力。” 黄仁勋回归英伟达 CEO 职位为本周初提供了暂时的喘息，但更广泛的担忧仍然存在，科技股占主导的纳斯达克和标普 500 指数仍处于自 2008 年以来最糟糕的 11 月走势轨道上。 芯片制造商引领了下跌，英伟达下跌 8.7%，更广泛的费城半导体指数下跌 7.3%。 其他巨型公司中， Alphabet 下跌 5%，Amazon 下跌 5.4%，Microsoft 和 Apple 分别下跌 3% 和 1.7%。 Anthropic 下跌 2.1%，周二收盘于 81.90 美元，低于上周 blockbuster 市场亮相后的 83 美元 IPO 价格。 纳斯达克 100 指数从其收盘高点短暂下跌 20%，接近熊市区域。 特朗普关税令华尔街惊恐 与此同时，美国提出了针对 14 个主要贸易伙伴的新关税，以应对其所谓的结构性过剩工业产能，重燃全球贸易紧张局势。 中国将面临最高的关税税率，拟议的 20% 过剩产能税是在美国总统唐纳德·特朗普第一任期期间征收的约 25% 关税之上的。 额外的关税可能会使投资者对利率维持更长时间的前景感到迷茫，因为通胀加速，油价因美伊战争而持续上涨。 关税担忧掩盖了经济数据，B. Riley Wealth 首席市场策略师 Art Hogan 说。 美国第三季度经济增长速度远超最初估计，而 10 月通胀进一步上升，强化了人们对美联储将于下个月再次在 2027 年初加息的预期。 美国东部时间上午 11 点 28 分，道琼斯工业平均指数下跌 602.93 点，或 1.21%，收于 49,415.77，标普 500 指数下跌 181.04 点，或 2.51%，收于 7,020.05，纳斯达克综合指数下跌 899.93 点，或 3.79%，收于 22,833.60。 标普 500 指数的科技板块以 5.2% 的跌幅引领损失，基准指数上的其他大多数板块也在负值区域交易。 在其他股票中，Dell Technologies 在提高年度收入和利润预测后仍下跌 7%。 rival PC 制造商 HP 在报告第四季度收入和利润高于分析师预期后上涨 11.7%。 美国市场将于周四感恩节当天关闭，当地时间，周五将缩短交易时间。 在纽约证券交易所，下跌的证券数量与上涨的证券数量之比为 2.05 比 1，在纳斯达克则为 2.97 比 1。 标普 500 指数创出 8 个新 52 周高点和 11 个新低点，而纳斯达克综合指数录得 17 个新高和 424 个新低。

What does this mean for the consensus process and reform? Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’? COP31 came to a dramatic close last weekend when a coalition of nations rejected the proposed “Antalya pact”, citing its failure to mention fossil fuels. The tense final moments and lack of a much-anticipated “pact” have sparked extensive media coverage around the world. Many commentators have rushed to label the COP31 outcome a “ failure ”, questioning what it means for the future of the UN climate process and a “ divided world ”. There has been much finger-pointing, with some outlets attributing COP31’s “collapse” to “ oil-rich nations ”, while others blame Europe’s “ reluctance ” to provide more climate finance. While it is not accurate to say there was “ no agreement ” at COP31, the media response demonstrates the complexity of the divergent views on display at the Antalya conference. In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome. What happened at COP31? What has the reaction to the presidency been? How has the role of oil-rich nations been portrayed? How has the role of developed nations been portrayed? How has the role of developing nations been portrayed? How has the role of China been portrayed? What does this mean for the consensus process and reform? Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’? What happened at COP31?  COP31 ended without agreement on a proposed “Antalya pact”, which had been pushed by the Turkey-Australia presidency. The final text was rejected by at least 32 countries, including the EU, the UK and some climate-vulnerable countries, in chaotic scenes as the talks overran by two days. An Irish Times editorial said the outcome was an “unprecedented ending of a COP without any agreement or roadmap forward”.  This view, while commonly expressed in the media, is incorrect.  As veteran “COP-watchers” explained for an article on CB Connect , the summit reached agreement on many decisions, even though the presidency’s “cover decision” failed.  Referring to the rejection of the cover decision, Melbourne University climate researchers Prof Jacqueline Peel and Prof Kathryn Bowen wrote in the Conversation that “these texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process”. .cb-membership-banner.alignfull { box-sizing: border-box; What has the reaction to the presidency been?  In the aftermath of COP31, commentators have critiqued decisions made by the presidency. An editorial in the Hindu noted that “usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations”, but said the COP31 leadership “thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings”.  Australian “president of negotiations” Chris Bowen has also faced criticism over how he managed competing interests at the summit. Similarly, climate-sceptic journalist Graham Lloyd wrote in the Australian that “globally, Bowen has embarrassed himself and diminished Australia’s reputation”.  For Australian news outlet Crikey , journalist Royce Kurmelovs said that Bowen “tried to run the world’s climate talks the way Labor [Australia’s ruling party] runs climate policy at home: quiet, pragmatic and without mentioning fossil fuels”, adding that “in Turkey, it didn’t work”. A commentary by journalist Xu Luyi in Chinese financial news outlet Caixin said that future COP presidencies should “distinguish achievable implementation measures from ambitions that lack a coalition capable of delivering them”. Separately, an editorial in the National – a UAE state-owned English-language daily newspaper – said “the next UN secretary general needs to restore the art of diplomacy”.  How has the role of oil-rich nations been portrayed?  In media coverage, much of the blame for the perceived failure of COP31 has been placed on oil-producing nations – particularly with the final cover decision draft containing no mention of fossil fuels.  Even before the summit had finished, Panama’s minister of environment Juan Carlos Navarro warned that the COP process was being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia”. After the talks had closed without a deal on the Antalya pact, a Guardian editorial said that responsibility lay with “petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels”, along with a lack of climate finance . The “fossil-fuel backsliding” was being led by a “Saudi-Russian coalition”, it said. A Bloomberg editorial also noted that the omission of fossil fuels from the decision text came “amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil fuel producers”. A Times editorial described oil-rich nations, “led by Saudi Arabia”, as the “culprits” for the lack of an agreement, because they “insisted on dropping a reference to phasing out hydrocarbons”. In the i newspaper , David Shukman, a former BBC News science editor, described a “deception” at the “heart” of the COP process: “This pattern of lobbying by oil-rich nations has become increasingly blatant and aggressive over more than three decades.” Despite signing up to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, the participation of the “oil-rich minority” has been “in name only”, wrote Shukman: “At more than a dozen of the UN’s giant conferences, I’ve seen for myself the tactics of trench warfare and how well they’ve worked. It’s why fossil fuels remain so dominant and why the climate is turning so hostile.” Writing for the Guardian , University College London’s Prof Bill McGuire warned that the COP process had been “deeply compromised” by the “major fossil-fuel producers”. For Al Jazeera , York University’s Prof Ilan Kapoor added that “fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall”. ( Reuters reported that, according to negotiators from Europe, small-island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa, Saudi officials had “regular access” to the summit’s presidents, “allowing them disproportionate influence”.) In Australian outlet Inside Story , the University of Sheffield’s Prof Michael Jacobs wrote that since “transitioning away from fossil fuels” language was included in COP28 , fossil-fuel producers “have been determined to ensure the phrase would never be used again”.  Nick O’Malley, national environment and climate editor for the Sydney Morning Herald , noted: “The tension between the action the world knows it must take on climate change and that which a handful of oil-rich nations will allow it to take has been growing for years.” At the summit itself, shortly after rejecting the cover decision on behalf of the EU, Irish environment minister Darragh O’Brien told Agence France-Presse that the talks had been “hijacked by some oil states”.  The Backchannel substack collated reactions from negotiators and observers. Among them, Dr Mary Robinson – former president of Ireland – warned of the “disturbing politicised attacks on [climate] science from those still clinging to fossil fuels and looking to sabotage climate action”. In contrast, an editorial in the National loosely described a failure of the talks to “bridge divisions over fossil-fuel language, carbon capture and adaptation finance in the final draft”. It added: “Unfortunately, the gap between countries – major emitters, energy producers and the more vulnerable nations demanding accessible funding – proved too wide to close.” How has the role of developed nations been portrayed?  Much of the commentary about developed countries’ role at COP31 focused on the EU and the UK blocking the final “Antalya pact”, due to its lack of language about fossil fuels. A cover-decision text without such language was “vehemently opposed by dozens of countries, including the EU delegation strongly led by [Irish] minister for climate Darragh O’Brien”, according to the Irish Times .  Similarly, an editorial in the UK’s Times concluded that “several countries, including the UK, rejected a draft omitting the not insignificant matter of winding down fossil-fuel use”. Peter Prengaman, climate news director for the Associated Press , wrote that the EU and its allies “were no longer willing” to leave out fossil-fuel language. (He noted that “top polluter” the US was not present at the summit.) Other media outlets took a more balanced approach to the role of developed nations at COP31. A Guardian editorial concluded:  “European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action.” Reflecting on the need for “funding to help the poorest countries adapt to global warming”, an editorial in Le Monde noted that “the most developed nations have been reluctant to increase their contributions, despite their historic responsibility for CO2 emissions”. An editorial in the Hindu stressed:  “It stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming.” Writing in US outlet Drilled , reporter Rishika Pardikar noted that “wealthy countries like Japan, the UK and Canada…largely aligned with the EU in opposing support mechanisms for developing countries like long-term finance, adaptation finance and just transition”. Climate campaigner John Gibbons wrote in the Irish Examiner that the EU was “right to reject” carbon capture and storage in the COP31 outcome, but accused O’Brien of “cosplay[ing] at being a progressive climate leader”, despite Ireland’s poor climate record. Many developed countries were not particularly vocal at COP31, and an editorial in Japan’s Yomiuri Shimbun lamented a general “low level of interest in and low priority given to global warming”. The editorial concluded: “It is hoped that Japan will continue to fulfill the practical roles expected of it and contribute to the international community in ways unique to Japan.” How has the role of developing nations been portrayed?  Equity, historical responsibility for climate change and a need for finance have all been portrayed at the centre of developing countries’ positions at COP31. A comment in the Hindu said that “India’s insistence on historical responsibility, climate finance and adaptation belongs at the centre of any credible plan to cut emissions”. It added that India had played a “constructive role” to “provide bridging language” in texts on adaptation and the just transition work programme. Down to Earth noted that “India has referred to historical responsibility in submissions at previous climate summits, but rarely with the emphasis evident” at COP31. Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative , told Radio France Internationale that those who criticise India’s opposition to fossil-fuel phaseout “need to acknowledge that there has been a lot of mistrust between India and developed countries”. Other developing countries also held firm, particularly on the issue of finance. Kenya’s the Star said the country had “drawn a firm line” at COP31 and would not “back down until an acceptable deal is secured on climate finance”. The outlet added that the country had “ruled out walking away from the negotiations”. Inter Press Service , a global south-focused news agency, noted that the “deadlock” at the talks leaves COP32 host Ethiopia “to pick up the pieces”. An editorial in the Mexican newspaper La Jornada called the failure to reach consensus “suicidal”, adding: “The conflict is far more complex than a mere opposition between the global north and south, or between hydrocarbon producers and consumers.” Indeed, some developing countries sided with developed countries in blocking the final passage of the Antalya pact.  The Fiji Times reported that Fiji “held the line in the final negotiating rooms”, joining the EU, the UK and several other Pacific countries in “refus[ing] to endorse a weakened compromise that avoided to mention fossil fuels [sic]”. It added: “Yet standing on principle carries heavy practical consequences…COP31’s breakdown is a sobering reminder that, while Fiji must keep fighting in global arenas, its sharpest shield remains regional solidarity and rapid, resilient action at home.” How has the role of China been portrayed? Major Chinese news outlets largely portrayed China as a constructive participant in the COP31 negotiations, a defender of multilateralism and an active advocate for international climate cooperation. State news agency Xinhua reported that “China acted responsibly and advanced the conference process, earning widespread recognition from all parties”. State broadcaster CCTV similarly said that the “international community recognised the positive role China played in addressing climate change”. People’s Daily , the official newspaper of the Communist Party of China, reported that China played a “constructive role” in building consensus and promoting cooperation. It quoted COP31 president Murat Kurum as saying that China was a “key participant” in the multilateral climate process and that its support was “crucial to the summit”. State news agency China News Service said that China demonstrated “ability to act” amid divisions at COP31, highlighting China’s participation in negotiations and initiatives on international cooperation in carbon credits and its climate actions in the global south.  Financial newspaper 21st Century Business Herald said that the Chinese delegation “actively participated in negotiations across all agenda items” and highlighted China’s efforts to advance practical cooperation on climate change.   Three of China’s main state media outlets, Xinhua , CCTV and People’s Daily , covered the COP31 outcome.  Xinhua said that climate multilateralism “moves forward under pressure” as COP31 concluded without a deal. Citing Chinese experts, Shanghai-based outlet the Paper reported that China, the African group and south-east Asian countries were among the parties “willing to accept a compromise [deal] to uphold multilateralism, despite being dissatisfied with the draft text”. CCTV reported that, although COP31 ended without adopting an “outcome document”, this did not mean international climate action had “come to a halt” or that previously agreed climate agreements and international promises would “automatically become invalid”.   State-run newspapers China Daily and the Global Times both published editorials on COP31.  China Daily argued that the COP31 “impasse” underscored the “need to strengthen multilateral cooperation”. It continued that China was “committed to addressing the climate crisis through real action.” The Global Times editorial, meanwhile, responded to criticism that China was “unwilling to take the lead”. It said: “With its own climate governance arrears unpaid, how can western media expect China to ‘pick up the tab’?” Regarding China’s role at COP31, several western news outlets’ coverage focused on its approach to climate diplomacy, trade and the proposed final agreement.  Ahead of the summit’s conclusion, Reuters cited diplomats and observers in reporting that China’s envoys to COP31 stuck to the country’s “accustomed low-key playbook”.  The Financial Times reported that China used the climate talks to “complain about tariffs on EVs and green energy products”.  On the final day of the summit, the Guardian said that China was among the parties that “did not object to the deal”.  Bloomberg also reported that while Chinese diplomats maintained a “relatively low profile”, its “world-leading” companies featured in China pavilion events.  Bloomberg continued: “at a United Nations climate conference that was low on delivery and high on dysfunction, China’s clean-technology companies showed that some aspects of the green transition are persevering despite geopolitical tensions.” What does this mean for the consensus process and reform?  In the aftermath of COP31, many commentators have called for a reform of the COP process. The European Commission is “drawing up plans to overhaul the UN climate summit process, warning that the current negotiating system risks becoming ineffective because a single country can block an agreement among nearly 200 parties”, according to Euronews .  Many other commentators shared the view that the COP process must be reformed. Marco Lambertini, convenor of the Nature Positive Initiative, said in Reuters : “We must be clear: reform remains essential. COPs are cumbersome, expensive, bureaucratic, environmentally unfriendly and frustratingly slow. The consensus rule – adopted in the climate and nature conferences – allows a handful of countries to dilute ambition in the main plenary deliberations. Too often, fossil fuel and agrochemical lobbies interfere with negotiations and obstruct progress. This must change.” Similarly, York University’s Kapoor said in Al Jazeera that the current system results in “an international forum in which the most reluctant participants can limit what everyone else is allowed to say, let alone do”.  The Associated Press ’ Prengaman wrote that “reforms floated over the years include shortening the conference from its current two weeks, limiting it just to delegates and reducing its overall size”. The Independent ’s climate correspondent, Nick Ferris, said the “collapse” of the talks “represents a shocking nadir in the history of COPs”, adding that “the process requires urgent reform”.  Similarly, Pilita Clark, the Financial Times associate editor and business columnist, said “the disaster that was the climate gathering in Antalya should prompt overdue reform”.  Justin Worland, a senior correspondent at Time , likened this year’s summit to the 2009 COP in Copenhagen. He added: “Following the defeat, negotiators went back to the drawing board and created the architecture that led to the Paris Agreement. Today, there’s another opportunity for reinvention.” (For more on COP reform, see Carbon Brief ’s interviews with 16 experts on the topic.) Could COP31 send a ‘positive signal’?  While many editorials lamented the failure of COP31 to agree on the Antalya pact, there were various articles that highlighted a more positive view.  In the Guardian , Dr Bill Hare , chief executive of Climate Analytics , wrote that COP31 was “a line in the sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no”. He continued:  “The [cover decision that parties] rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.” Others shared the view that numerous countries rejecting the cover decision due to its failure to mention fossil fuels could be seen as a significant moment of pushback. In an interview in Le Monde , Prof Johan Rockström , director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany, said that it is “better to have this kind of crisis and to do something good with it, rather than having a watered-down agreement”. He added:  “It will have a very positive signal: It means that the world is taking risks seriously. The world is taking science seriously.” An editorial in Bloomberg stated that COP31 should “serve as a call for action”, pushing like-minded governments to continue working together to make progress. It added:  “The outcome at COP31, discouraging as it was, strongly suggests that much of the world remains committed to fighting climate change. More than 100 governments, led by the EU, opposed a final declaration that – amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil-fuel producers – omitted any reference to the transition away from fossil fuels.”  In Reuters , columnist Antony Currie wrote that the failure to adopt the cover decision could in fact be “healthy”. Elsewhere, in Inside Story , the University of Sheffield’s r Jacobs argued that “this COP’s failure might have been what the world needed”.  Related CB Live: Carbon Brief journalists discuss key COP31 outcomes 24.11.2026 COP31 Antalya COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya 24.11.2026 COP31 Antalya COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya 23.11.2026 COP31 Antalya Revealed: Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are largest CO2 exporters of all time 17.11.2026 Emissions The post Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’? appeared first on Carbon Brief .

title: Italian Navy’s First ‘Full’ PPA Giovanni delle Bande Nere Demonstrates BMD Capabilities
zh_title: 意大利海军第一艘“完整”PPA Giovanni delle Bande Nere 展示弹道导弹防御能力
summary: 在意大利海军 BMD 的一个重大里程碑中，第一艘“全”MPCS/PPA Giovanni delle Bande Nere 使用 Aster 30 拦截了一枚高速弹道导弹。Giovanni delle Bande Nere (P 434) 是 Thaon di Revel 级的第四艘单位，也是第一艘 MPCS/PPA（多用途战斗舰/Pattugliatore Polivalente d’Altura），由 Fincantieri 建造并交付莱昂纳多的“PPA Full”多角色配置具有增强型综合防空和导弹防御（IAMD）以及反潜战能力，是意大利海军成功实现自主作战的首要作战平台
content:
在意大利海军 BMD 的一个重大里程碑中，第一艘“全”MPCS/PPA Giovanni delle Bande Nere 使用 Aster 30 拦截了一枚高速弹道导弹。Giovanni delle Bande Nere (P 434) 是 Thaon di Revel 级的第四艘单位，也是第一艘 MPCS/PPA（多用途战斗舰/Pattugliatore Polivalente d’Altura），由 Fincantieri 建造并交付据意大利海军社交媒体报道，“PPA Full”多角色配置具有增强型综合防空和导弹防御（IAMD）以及莱昂纳多的反潜作战能力，是意大利海军的首要作战平台，可在实弹射击过程中成功实现从探测到拦截“高速弹道导弹”的自主交战。 Bande Nere 最近完成了在印度-太平洋地区为期六个月的作战部署，并于 2026 年 11 月 13 日返回其位于塔兰托海军基地的母港。这一成就使 Marina Militare 跻身能够直接应对海上弹道威胁的海军俱乐部之列。 Bande Nere MPCS/PPA Full已在印太地区进行了为期六个月的作战部署，参加了环太平洋军演和太平洋龙2026演习。 （美国海军摄影：大众传播专家一级 Erik Melgar）“多任务战舰 Giovanni delle Bande Nere 成功地进行了一次高度复杂的演习，探测、拦截和压制高速弹道导弹。
11 月 20 日，意大利海军在其 X 社交媒体账户上表示：“成功的链条包括：精确探测和跟踪、使用舰载作战管理系统计算发射解决方案、交战和完美拦截。”该公告还附有从 Bande Nere MPCS/PPA 快速连发两枚 MBDA Aster 防空导弹进行实弹射击的视频，以及操作员在作战作战中心控制台上的图像。尽管目前尚未提供有关实弹射击的更多细节，但据报道，根据《海军新闻》收集的信息和 CMS 控制台上显示的地图，“班德尼尔”号船员在过去几周内在希腊克里特岛的北约导弹发射装置（NAMFI）海上射击场进行了现场交战，据知情人士透露，这项活动是由意大利海军 MPCS/PPA 船员在去年 11 月 13 日抵达其母港之前进行的，当时是在印度-太平洋地区进行了六个月的作战部署返回途中。 《海军新闻》了解到，如此高要求的实弹射击演习并不是在“内雷号”号于2026年5月出发执行作战部署之前计划的，而是在任务期间安排和准备的，进一步证实了意大利海军在快速变化的作战环境中规划和应对紧急作战需求的灵活性。
意大利海上防御和国家科技工业的非凡作战成就！这一成功立即将 #MarinaMilitare 打造成一支能够直接对抗海上弹道威胁的海军陆战队精锐部队，保证…… pic.twitter.com/46MWq5FjXD — Marina Militare (@ItalianNavy) 2026 年 11 月 20 日 自 Fincantieri 于 10 月交付以来，第一艘全战斗配置的 PPA 接受了对具有 IAMD 和多角色能力的新战斗和武器系统套件的广泛资格和操作评估

【原文 English Original】
In a major Italian Navy BMD milestone, the first ‘Full’ MPCS/PPA Giovanni delle Bande Nere intercepted a high-speed ballistic missile using Aster 30. The Giovanni delle Bande Nere (P 434), the fourth unit of the Thaon di Revel-class and the first MPCS/PPA (Multi-Purpose Combat Ship/Pattugliatore Polivalente d’Altura) built by Fincantieri and delivered in the “PPA Full” multi-role configuration with enhanced integrated air and missile defence (IAMD) alongside anti-submarine warfare capabilities by Leonardo, is the premiere combatant platform of the Italian Navy to achieve a successful autonomous engagement from detection to interception of a ‘high-speed ballistic missile’ during a live firing, according to Italian Navy social media. The Bande Nere has recently completed its six-month operational deployment in the Indo-Pacific region, with the return to its homeport at Taranto naval base on 13 November 2026. This achievement places the Marina Militare among the club of navies capable of countering ballistic threats directly from the sea. The Bande Nere MPCS/PPA Full has conducted a six-month operational deployment in the Indo-Pacific region participating to RIMPAC and PACIFIC DRAGON 2026 exercises. (U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Erik Melgar) “The multi-mission combat vessel Giovanni delle Bande Nere successfully conducted a highly complex exercise, detecting, intercepting and neutralising a high-speed ballistic missile. The chain of success: precision detection and tracking, calculation of the firing solution using the onboard Combat Management System, engagement and flawless interception,” said the Italian Navy with her X social media account on 20 November. The announcement was accompanied by a video of the live firing with a ‘ripple’ of two MBDA Aster air defence missiles in rapid sequence from the Bande Nere MPCS/PPA alongside images of operators at their consoles in the combat operational centre. Although no further details were provided so far about the live firing, according to information collected by Naval News and the maps displayed on the CMS consoles, the live engagement was conducted by the Bande Nere crew in the last couple of weeks on the at-sea firing range area of the NATO Missile Firing Installation (NAMFI) on the island of Crete in Greece. This activity, according to informed sources was carried out by the Italian Navy MPCS/PPA crew before reaching its homeport last 13 November, on the way back from the six-month operational deployment in the Indo-Pacific region. Naval News understood that such demanding live firing exercise wasn’t planned before the departure of the Bande Nere for the operational deployment in May 2026, but was scheduled and prepared during the mission, further confirming the Italian Navy planning flexibility and response to urgent operational needs in a fast changing operational environment. Un traguardo operativo straordinario per la difesa marittima italiana e per l'industria tecnologica nazionale! Questo successo proietta da subito la #MarinaMilitare in un'élite ristretta di Marine capaci di contrastare minacce balistiche direttamente dal mare, garantendo la… pic.twitter.com/46MWq5FjXD — Marina Militare (@ItalianNavy) November 20, 2026 The first PPA in the full combat configuration was subjected to an extensive qualification and operational evaluation of the new combat and weapon system suite with IAMD and multirole capabilities since its delivery by Fincantieri in October 2024. The Bande Nere launched its first Aster 30 missile in February 2025 and participated to the international IAMD Formidable Shield followed by the French Navy-lead Polaris exercises in the Atlantic Ocean in the same year, before conducting the six-month operational deployment in the Indo-Pacific region in 2026. Here, it joined the US Navy-lead RIMPAC worldwide largest naval exercise and the IAMD-dedicated Pacific Dragon exercise. According to the information released by the Italian Navy social media and the associated video, the Bande Nere crew successfully employed the ship combat system centred on the Leonardo SADOC 5 CMS with IAMD capabilities and the Dual Band Radar (DBR) incorporating the four fixed-faces (4FF) AESA GaN-based C-band Kronos Quad and the 4FF AESA X-band GaAs-based Star Fire systems, alongside the integrated electronic warfare suite (IEWS) by ELT Group, to detect, track and generate the firing solution to successfully engaged the ballistic target with the MBDA Italia SAAM ESD (Surface Anti-Air Missile – Extended Self Defence) PPA air defence missile system. Centred on two Naval Group A50 8-cell vertical launch systems (VLS) for the family of Aster surface-to-air munitions, C2 and firing units, the SAAM ESD PPA system launched a ‘ripple’ of two Aster 30 missiles to intercept and successfully neutralize the ballistic threat. No indication was provided on the missile type, but the longer range Aster 30 is used for the ATBM mission as identified by the video still frames. Based on previous information released on the contracts and deliveries of Aster 30 munitions to Italian Navy, Naval News understood the Bande Nere MPCS/PPA employed the standard Aster 30 munition, which represents the inventory weapon for the Italian Navy. If officially confirmed, it represent a further testimony of the Aster 30 capabilities against ballistic threats, after the first engagements conducted in 2024 by the French Navy in the Red Sea. This until both Navies will receive the Aster 30 Block 1 NT munition version specifically developed to counter ballistic as well as hypersonic missile threats in addition to conventional ones including aircraft, drones and cruise missiles. An operator at a console of the Leonardo SADOC 4 CMS of the Bande Nere MPCS/PPA during the live firing at the NAMFI at-sea range area. (Photo credit: Italian Navy) “An extraordinary operational milestone for Italian maritime defence and the national industry. This success places the Marina Militare among an elite group of navies capable of countering ballistic threats directly from the sea, ensuring the stability and security of maritime routes in the Mediterranean and beyond,” highlighted the Italian Navy with the same statement on its X social media account. No further information were released on the firing theme and used ballistic target, but according to the NAMFI website, anti-tactical ballistic missile (ATBM) firings are the most important an demanding activities conducted on the international military range managed by the Hellenic Ministry of Defence, since the firsts were carried out by German and Netherlands Air Defence Units at the same facilities on October 2007, being an European first. Besides such land-based activities, which are conducted in support of Patriot ground based air defence systems, NAMFI range has the capability and experience to also host naval (platform) firings against ballistic missile targets, as demonstrated by the successful activities of the Italian Navy MPCS/PPA. The ATBM firings are conducted for the air defence units “against the Supersonic Target (STAR) missile provided by TMD target company, according to NAMFI website. Naval News understood the target was fired from a land site, while the ship was operating in high sea inside the at-sea wide range area. The NAMFI range includes a 14,440 square kilometres of land, sea and air space with an area at sea 166 km long and 87 km wide (expandable to 226 km in length under certain conditions for a total of 19,660 square kilometres) which stretches along the northern coast of Crete island. This area is divided in 3 subareas (A, B and C), it is crossed by air corridors, it affects two international airport terminals (Heraklion and Chania) and four main national ports (Souda, Rethimno, Heraklion, Santorini). The successful autonomous engagement of a target representing a tactical ballistic missile not only adds the Italian Navy to the club of naval forces capable of defending the national territory, fleet and allied ships against this threats but also testimony the capabilities reached by the Italian defence and naval industry in the IAMD sector. The combat and weapon system of the MPCS/PPA in the full combat configuration is planned to equip the whole class of ships as well as the FREEM EVO platform and and are offered on the international market, where the launch customer is expected to be the Portuguese MoD and Navy with the national FREMM EVO procurement programme, but thanks to its scalability and modularity can be integrated on other naval platforms offered by Fincantieri but also other shipbuilders. The post Italian Navy’s First ‘Full’ PPA Giovanni delle Bande Nere Demonstrates BMD Capabilities appeared first on Naval News .

Chinese v American Views on WAR with Taiwan
Posted Aug 14, 2026 by Martin Armstrong |
The Center for Strategic and International Studies conducted an extraordinary survey of 64 leading experts on China, Taiwan, and cross-Strait relations, including 28 former senior U.S. government officials, 23 former government policy and intelligence analysts, and 13 academics and think-tank experts. What their answers reveal is not that China is preparing to invade Taiwan tomorrow, as the neocons would like everyone to believe, but that Beijing remains willing to wait so long as nobody crosses the line of formal Taiwanese independence. Some 84% said Beijing is willing to wait for unification but will not accept the status quo permanently, while only 10% believed China seeks unification at the earliest opportunity. Not one of the 64 experts believed Beijing would ever accept an independent Taiwan.
This is precisely why Taiwan has become so dangerous. The West keeps portraying the conflict as if Xi Jinping wakes up every morning staring at a calendar trying to decide when to launch an amphibious invasion. Yet 83% of these experts said China did not plan to use significant kinetic force against Taiwan by 2027, and 80% said China’s enormous 2022 military exercises did not indicate Beijing had accelerated its timetable. Only 6% of respondents outside the former senior government group saw 2027 as a hard deadline, while not one former senior U.S. official did. The obsession with 2027 has nevertheless become extremely useful for the military establishment because every supposed deadline becomes another justification for weapons, deployments, bases, and spending.
The survey found that 44% believed Beijing has a hard deadline of 2049, the centennial of the People’s Republic, while 42% believed China could wait indefinitely provided unification remains possible. This is an important distinction because China thinks in terms of generations while Western politicians think in terms of the next election. Beijing does not need to invade Taiwan if economic, political, and military pressure can gradually change the situation in its favor. Only 20% of those surveyed believed China even possessed a coherent roadmap for peaceful unification, which tells us this is not some perfectly scripted invasion plan sitting in Xi’s desk drawer.
Where the numbers become alarming is not an unprovoked invasion but what happens when politicians begin crossing China’s red lines. More than three-quarters of the experts, 77%, believed China would invade within six months if Taiwan formally declared independence. Among former senior U.S. officials, that number was 79%. Even some of those who did not expect an immediate invasion believed Beijing would respond with a blockade or enormous military exercises. This is why politicians encouraging Taiwan toward formal independence are playing with the lives of 23 million people. They can deliver all the speeches they want about democracy from Washington, London, or Brussels, but they will not be the civilians sitting underneath the missiles if their political experiment goes wrong.
Not one expert believed an explicit American commitment to defend Taiwan would cause China to invade immediately, but 64% believed Beijing would respond strongly enough to provoke a U.S.-China or China-Taiwan crisis, while another 31% expected a more limited negative response. Only two of the 64 experts believed formally committing America to Taiwan’s defense would actually deter China from using force because Beijing already assumes that the United States will intervene anyway.
A direct invasion is not even the most likely path toward conflict. Only 8% of the experts described an amphibious invasion within ten years as likely, while 63% called it possible and 27% unlikely. Force short of invasion received much higher probabilities, with 52% saying deliberate escalation such as a blockade was likely or very likely. An accidental military incident was considered even more dangerous, with 34% saying a collision or accident around the Taiwan Strait was likely and another 22% calling it very likely. When warships and aircraft from opposing nuclear powers continually operate around the same small body of water, war does not require some grand master plan. It requires one mistake followed by politicians who refuse to back down.
A later CSIS survey of American and Taiwanese experts reinforces that point. Roughly 90% of U.S. experts and 62% of Taiwanese experts believed China already possessed the capability to impose a law-enforcement-led quarantine that substantially reduces trade into Taiwan. Around 80% of American experts and 60% of Taiwanese experts believed Beijing could execute a PLA blockade, while Taiwanese experts were considerably more skeptical that China could successfully carry out an invasion. If Beijing wanted to coerce Taiwan during the following five years, experts considered a quarantine the most likely option. If China decided it wanted immediate unification, however, approximately 80% regarded a highly kinetic joint blockade as likely or very likely.
This is where the economic consequences become enormous because Taiwan does not need to be invaded for the world economy to be thrown into chaos. A quarantine or blockade would immediately threaten shipping, insurance, semiconductor supply chains, electronics, automobiles, communications equipment, and virtually every modern industry dependent upon advanced chips. The later CSIS survey found most American and Taiwanese experts did not believe Taiwan could withstand a Chinese blockade for longer than three months without substantial U.S. intervention. Washington would then face the decision nobody wants to discuss honestly: accept China’s blockade or attempt to break it militarily and risk direct war between two nuclear powers.
Taiwan is also the world’s semiconductor pressure point. The island’s importance to advanced chip manufacturing means a serious blockade would not remain a regional event. Factories thousands of miles away could discover that a conflict they thought had nothing to do with them suddenly prevents them from obtaining critical components. Markets would begin repricing the risk immediately, shipping premiums would explode, companies would scramble for inventory, and governments would discover once again how fragile global supply chains have become. This is why capital will react long before politicians formally declare that a war has begun.
What I find particularly revealing in the later CSIS survey is the difference between American confidence and Taiwanese confidence in Washington. An astonishing 96% of American experts were completely or moderately confident that the United States would intervene militarily if China invaded Taiwan during the following five years. Taiwanese experts were less confident in American intervention and considerably less confident that U.S. allies would join the fight. It is always easier for people thousands of miles away to be certain about somebody else’s war.
This is precisely why Taiwan remains one of the critical geopolitical pressure points as we move toward 2029. The danger is not simply that China arbitrarily decides to invade. The greater danger is escalation, miscalculation, political promises that cannot be withdrawn, and Western policymakers convincing themselves that every additional provocation somehow produces deterrence. China has made its position on formal independence perfectly clear, and even the experts inside the Western foreign-policy establishment overwhelmingly acknowledge that Beijing would react with force if that line were crossed.
If Taiwan declares formal independence, 77% of the experts surveyed believed China would invade within six months. That is not a statistic policymakers should treat as another war-game scenario. It is a warning about what happens when politicians deliberately remove the ambiguity that has helped keep the peace.

title: 神舟二十四號成功發射 首位巴基斯坦航天員登中國「天宮」意味什麼？
summary: 神舟二十四號成功發射 首位巴基斯坦航天員登中國「天宮」意味什麼？ - BBC News 中文 中國神舟二十四號自中國西北部戈壁沙漠發射升空，執行將三名航天員送入太空的任務。 其中一人是來自巴基斯坦的穆罕默德·齊尚·阿里（Muhammad Zeeshan Ali），40歲的他創造歷史，成為首名登上中國「天宮」太空站的外籍航天員，將與兩名中國航天員湯洪波及武毅一同執行任務。 對阿里而言，這是巴基斯坦的榮耀時刻；對中國而言，則是其與美國爭奪太空主導地位競賽中的又一進展。 新華社報道
content:
神舟二十四號成功發射 首位巴基斯坦航天員登中國「天宮」意味什麼？ - BBC News 中文
中國神舟二十四號自中國西北部戈壁沙漠發射升空，執行將三名航天員送入太空的任務。
其中一人是來自巴基斯坦的穆罕默德·齊尚·阿里（Muhammad Zeeshan Ali），40歲的他創造歷史，成為首名登上中國「天宮」太空站的外籍航天員，將與兩名中國航天員湯洪波及武毅一同執行任務。
對阿里而言，這是巴基斯坦的榮耀時刻；對中國而言，則是其與美國爭奪太空主導地位競賽中的又一進展。
新華社報道，國家主席習近平與巴基斯坦總統扎爾達里就中巴航天員執行聯合飛行任務互致賀電。
圖像加註文字，11月25日：2026年11月25日，中國航天員湯洪波、武毅與巴基斯坦航天員穆罕默德·齊尚·阿里在中國酒泉出席「神舟24號」乘組的歡送儀式。
阿里在早前記者會談及這次任務對自己及巴基斯坦的重要意義，他表示，「我肩負著巴基斯坦的名字，也肩負著2.5億巴基斯坦人民的期望。」
他又指，「對每一位在觀看這次任務的孩子，我想說，抬頭看看天空，記住我就在那裡，帶著你們的夢想一起飛翔。」
BBC駐中國記者碧嘉蘭分析，這次任務不僅是一項科學成就，也是一項地緣政治宣示。
中國首次安排外籍航天員進入太空，主要有兩個目的：科學合作與外交影響力。
阿里將在為期數天的短期軌道飛行期間，進行一系列生物科技及光合微生物領域的實驗，其後返回地球。
北京希望藉這次飛行進一步鞏固與伊斯蘭堡的關係，尤其是在兩國正紀念建交75周年之際。
中國多年來已向太空計劃投入數以十億美元計資金，而其重點項目天宮太空站目前由三人航天員團隊駐守，並約每六個月輪換一次。
如今，中國希望向外界展示，天宮太空站有能力成為國際科研平台，而非僅供中國使用的設施。
與此同時，北京試圖把自己塑造成美國主導太空計劃以外的重要替代選擇，並計劃於2030年前首次把中國航天員送上月球。
建立國際合作夥伴關係有助提升影響力和國際公信力。因此，中國希望透過這次任務傳達一個訊息：中國也能為其他國家提供將航天員送入太空的機會。
圖像加註文字，巴基斯坦航天員穆罕默德·齊尚·阿里（Muhammad Zeeshan Ali）出席記者會。
由於巴基斯坦沒有自行將航天員送上太空的運載工具，因此這次任務所有關鍵環節都依賴中國提供支援。
阿里與另一名進入神舟二十四號最終遴選階段的巴基斯坦候選人庫拉姆·達烏德（Khurram Dawood），均在中國接受訓練，並在中國專家的指導下於中國太空站模擬設施進行相關工作。
神舟二十四號於週三早上8時多發射升空，中國官方估計，飛船從發射到與天宮太空站對接大約需要三個半小時。
據路透社報道，阿里將在天宮太空站停留約一周，遠短於中國航天員一般約六個月的駐站時間。他其後將與兩名今年5月較早前抵達太空站的中國航天員一同返回地球。至於中國航天員湯洪波、武毅，則將與神舟二十三號乘組成員朱楊柱一同在天宮太空站駐留六個月。朱楊柱目前正研究人體如何適應長時間太空生活。
神舟二十四號乘組在太空期間將進行多項實驗及技術測試，涵蓋太空生命科學（space life sciences）、航天醫學（aerospace medicine）及燃燒科學（combustion science）。
例如，研究人員將探討太空環境如何影響血管老化（vascular ageing）等生理過程，希望有助研發新的預防及治療策略。
來自巴基斯坦的阿里則將負責研究細菌光合作用（photosynthesis in bacteria）、太空輻射及微重力環境對藜麥種子的影響。
迄今全球約有50個國家曾把本國公民送入太空，但只有美國、中國及俄羅斯能夠依靠自主研發的太空船完成這項任務。在此背景下，中國邀請巴基斯坦派遣航天員前往天宮太空站，被視為一項具有重要意義的發展。
阿里曾在空軍服役，對為這次歷史性任務作準備所需的高強度體能及技術訓練並不陌生。他是首位接受專業航天員訓練後進入太空的巴基斯坦人。
由於太空船上的所有開關、軟件系統、操作程序及語音廣播均以普通話運作，阿里不僅要掌握日常會話，還必須熟悉大量專業技術詞彙。
據路透社報道，阿里在北京接受為期七個月的密集中文培訓，期間除了學習普通話，也學唱中文歌曲及學習中國詩詞，並接觸書法和乒乓球等活動。
根據多家媒體報道，阿里表示：「我接受過多種訓練，包括離心機訓練、救援與生存訓練，以及緊急程序訓練，但老實說，最大的挑戰是掌握中文。」
這項語言訓練被視為他能夠參與神舟二十四號任務的重要一環，因為整個飛行及太空站操作系統均以中文為工作語言。
2023年10月，常駐摩納哥的巴基斯坦裔極地探險家納米拉·薩利姆（Namira Salim）曾乘搭維珍銀河（Virgin Galactic）的Galactic 04任務進入太空。她於2006年購買這趟商業太空飛行的船票，票價為20萬美元。
所謂次軌道飛行（suborbital flight），是指飛行器雖然到達外太空，但飛行速度未達到維持環繞地球運行所需的軌道速度（orbital velocity）。
Galactic 04任務共有六名乘員，包括三名維珍銀河員工，以及三名太空旅客；以廣義而言，薩利姆是首位進入太空的巴基斯坦人；阿里則是首名巴基斯坦專業航天員。
我們使用了人工智能協助翻譯這篇文章，它的原文是英文。在發佈之前，BBC記者檢查了翻譯的內容。

title: Tentara Nasional Indonesia Angkatan Laut, U.S. Navy commence CARAT Indonesia 2026
zh_title: 印度尼西亚国家陆军海军和美国海军启动 CARAT Indonesia 2026
summary: 2026 年 11 月 25 日，印度尼西亚泗水（2026 年 11 月 25 日）——来自美国第七舰队和印度尼西亚国家海军部队 (TNI-AL) 的海防部队于 11 月 25 日在泗水举行会议，开始印度尼西亚海上合作准备和训练 (CARAT)。第 32 届 CARAT 印度尼西亚演习以开幕式启动，以美国和印度尼西亚之间之前的海上演习和行动为基础。 CARAT是一项海上演习，旨在促进地区安全合作，维护和加强海上伙伴关系，增强参演部队之间的互操作性
content:
2026 年 11 月 25 日

印度尼西亚泗水（2026 年 11 月 25 日）——来自美国第七舰队和印度尼西亚国家海军部队 (TNI-AL) 的海防部队于 11 月 25 日在泗水召开会议，开始印度尼西亚海上合作准备和训练 (CARAT)。

第 32 届 CARAT 印度尼西亚演习以开幕式启动，以美国和印度尼西亚之间之前的海上演习和行动为基础。 CARAT是一项海上演习，旨在促进地区安全合作，维护和加强海上伙伴关系，增强参演部队之间的互操作性。

美国驻泗水总领事克里斯·格林表示：“CARAT 代表了美国和印度尼西亚共同致力于促进整个印度-太平洋地区的海上安全和战备。” “30 多年来，CARAT 不断增强我们在广泛的海军能力领域并肩工作的能力。”
第 77 特遣部队 (CTF) 指挥官的复仇者级反水雷舰 USS Warrior (MCM 10) 于 11 月 25 日抵达印度尼西亚，启动初步活动。演习的海上阶段还将有来自 CTF-72 的一架 P-8A 海神海上巡逻和侦察机、三艘 TNI-AL 西格玛级护卫舰、法尼级反水雷舰 KRI Pulau Fani (MCMV 731) 和 KRI Pulau Fanildo (MCMV 732)、两架空客 AS656 Panther 直升机和一架 TNI-AL CN 235 飞机。 TNI-AL。此次迭代的海上阶段将以反潜战演习、水雷对抗最佳实践以及水面行动小组协调来进行跨部队指挥和控制为特色。

支持 CARAT 印度尼西亚 2026 的其他人员和工作人员包括美国第七舰队中队第 7 驱逐舰中队 (DESRON) 的指挥官，以及来自 CTF-73、CTF-75 和太平洋海军信息战中心的主题专家。主题专家交流 (SMEE) 主题将包括航空、网络、打捞潜水、爆炸物处理和 **U.S.-TNI-AL** 联合音乐表演。在泗水岸上举行的 SMEE 将通过建立人与人之间的关系来促进信息共享并促进海上互操作性。
“我们感谢印度尼西亚合作伙伴在泗水的热情欢迎和热情款待，”CTF-76 参谋长兼代表团团长美国海军上尉阿方扎·怀特 (Alfonza White) 说。 “CARAT 加强了我们的协调，建立了互信，并帮助我们维护了一个自由开放的印太地区。”

CARAT是一项长期演习系列，旨在增强美国及其伙伴部队共同行动应对该地区共同海上挑战的能力。

作为美国海军在东南亚前沿部署的DESRON，DESRON-7担任东南亚作战地区指定舰艇的主要战术和作战指挥官。

美国第七舰队是海军最大的前沿部署编号舰队，经常与盟友和伙伴互动和行动，以维护自由开放的印度太平洋地区。

【原文 English Original】
25 November 2026

SURABAYA, Indonesia (Nov. 25, 2026) — Maritime defense forces from U.S. 7th Fleet and Tentara Nasional Indonesia Angkatan Laut (TNI-AL) convened in Surabaya, Nov. 25, to commence Cooperation Afloat Readiness and Training (CARAT) Indonesia.

The 32nd iteration of CARAT Indonesia launched with an opening ceremony, building upon previous maritime exercises and operations between the U.S. and Indonesia. CARAT is a maritime exercise designed to promote regional security cooperation, maintain and strengthen maritime partnerships, and enhance interoperability among participating forces.

“CARAT represents a commitment shared by the United States and Indonesia to promote maritime security and readiness across the Indo-Pacific,” said Chris Green, U.S. Consul General in Surabaya. “After more than 30 years, CARAT continues to enhance our ability to work side-by-side across a wide range of naval competencies.”

Avenger-class mine countermeasures ship USS Warrior (MCM 10) from Commander, Task Force (CTF) 77 arrived in Indonesia, Nov. 25, to kick off preliminary events. The sea-phase of the exercise will also feature a P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol and reconnaissance aircraft from CTF-72, as well as three TNI-AL Sigma-class corvettes, Fani-class mine countermeasures vessels KRI Pulau Fani (MCMV 731) and KRI Pulau Fanildo (MCMV 732), two Airbus AS656 Panther helicopters, and one TNI-AL CN 235 aircraft from TNI-AL. The sea-phase of this iteration will feature anti-submarine warfare drills, mine countermeasures best practices, and surface action group coordination to exercise command and control across units.

Additional personnel and staff supporting CARAT Indonesia 2026 include Commander, Destroyer Squadron (DESRON) 7, the U.S. 7th Fleet Band, and subject matter experts from CTF-73, CTF-75, and Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific. Subject matter expert exchange (SMEE) topics will include aviation, cyber, salvage diving, explosive ordnance disposal, and **U.S.–TNI-AL** combined musical performances. The SMEEs, held ashore in Surabaya, will facilitate information-sharing and promote interoperability at sea through building people-to-people relationships.

“We are grateful to our Indonesian partners for their warm welcome and hospitality in Surabaya,” said U.S. Navy Capt. Alfonza White, chief of staff, CTF-76, and head of delegation. “CARAT strengthens our coordination, builds mutual trust, and helps us preserve a free and open Indo-Pacific.”

CARAT is a long-standing exercise series designed to enhance U.S. and partner forces abilities to operate together in response to shared maritime challenges in the region.

As the U.S. Navy’s forward-deployed DESRON in Southeast Asia, DESRON-7 serves as the primary tactical and operational commander of assigned ships in the Southeast Asia area of operations.

U.S. 7th Fleet, the Navy’s largest forward-deployed numbered fleet, routinely interacts and operates with allies and partners in preserving a free and open Indo-Pacific.

The Trump administration is trying to protect Golden Dome and other priority programs as the budget remains uncertain.

summary: 澳大利亚悉尼——陆军对话是一个定期举行的论坛，使参与国能够协调竞选工作、讨论行动优先事项并寻找加强合作的机会。该论坛包括高级领导人参与活动和工作组，以推动整个印太地区的陆军活动。太平洋陆军在悉尼举行的陆军对话技术工作组期间加强合作 来自澳大利亚、美国、日本和菲律宾的高级领导人和代表团成员出席了破冰活动
content:
澳大利亚悉尼——

陆军对话是一个定期举行的论坛，使参与国能够协调战役工作、讨论行动优先事项并确定加强合作的机会。该论坛包括高级领导人参与活动和工作组，以推动整个印太地区的陆军活动。

太平洋陆军在悉尼陆军对话技术工作组期间加强合作 摄影：CPL Hamid Farahani

2026 年 11 月 17 日，陆军对话 - 技术工作组期间，来自澳大利亚、美国、日本和菲律宾的高级领导人和代表团成员出席了在悉尼维多利亚军营军官食堂举行的破冰活动。*** 本地字幕 *** 参加陆军对话 - 技术工作组的高级军事领导人和代表在正式讨论之前出席了在悉尼维多利亚军营举行的破冰活动。该活动为来自澳大利亚、美国、日本和菲律宾的代表提供了建立专业关系并讨论共同安全利益的机会。陆军对话-技术工作组是参与陆军的一个重要论坛，旨在加强合作并改善整个印太地区未来行动、活动和投资的同步性。
澳大利亚陆军主办了为期四天的论坛，汇聚了代表四个盟国和伙伴国的六个军种的人员：澳大利亚陆军、日本陆上自卫队、菲律宾陆军、菲律宾海军陆战队、美国太平洋海军陆战队和美国太平洋陆军。与会者的重点是在 2027 年及以后调整战略态势、提高作战持久力以及增强多边地面力量能力。

> “我们通过陆军对话等论坛建立的关系增强了我们在最重要的时候共同行动的能力，”

美国太平洋海军陆战队副司令马修·T·莫厄里少将说道。

> “将四个国家和六个军种聚集在一起，使我们能够更好地调整优先事项，提高互操作性，并在共同计划下作为一支统一的力量开展行动。这种合作加强了我们的集体准备，并加强了我们对自由开放的印太地区的承诺。”

太平洋陆军在悉尼陆军对话技术工作组期间加强合作 摄影：CPL Hamid Farahani
2026 年 11 月 17 日，陆军对话 - 技术工作组期间，来自澳大利亚、美国、日本和菲律宾的高级领导人和代表团成员出席了在悉尼维多利亚军营军官食堂举行的破冰活动。*** 本地字幕 *** 参加陆军对话 - 技术工作组的高级军事领导人和代表在正式讨论之前出席了在悉尼维多利亚军营举行的破冰活动。该活动为来自澳大利亚、美国、日本和菲律宾的代表提供了建立专业关系并讨论共同安全利益的机会。陆军对话-技术工作组是参与陆军的一个重要论坛，旨在加强合作并改善整个印太地区未来行动、活动和投资的同步性。

SYDNEY, Australia --

Land Forces Dialogue is a recurring forum that enables participating nations to coordinate campaign efforts, discuss operational priorities and identify opportunities to enhance cooperation. The forum includes senior leader engagements and working groups that advance land force activities across the Indo-Pacific.

Pacific Land Forces Strengthen Cooperation During Land Forces Dialogue Technical Working Group in Sydney Photo by CPL Hamid Farahani

Senior leaders and delegation members from Australia, the United States, Japan and the Philippines attend an ice-breaker function at the Victoria Barracks Officers' Mess, Sydney, during the Land Force Dialogue – Technical Working Group on 17 November 2026. *** Local Caption *** Senior military leaders and delegates participating in the Land Force Dialogue – Technical Working Group attended an ice-breaker function at Victoria Barracks, Sydney, ahead of formal discussions. The function provided an opportunity for delegates from Australia, the United States, Japan and the Philippines to build professional relationships and discuss shared security interests. The Land Force Dialogue – Technical Working Group serves as a key forum for participating land forces to strengthen cooperation and improve synchronisation of future operations, activities and investments throughout the Indo-Pacific region.

The Australian Army hosted the four-day forum, which brought together personnel from six military services representing four allied and partner nations: the Australian Army, Japan Ground Self-Defense Force, Philippine Army, Philippine Marine Corps, U.S. Marine Corps Forces Pacific, and U.S. Army Pacific. Participants focused on aligning strategic posture, improving operational endurance, and enhancing multilateral land power capabilities through calendar year 2027 and beyond.

> “The relationships we build through forums like the Land Forces Dialogue strengthen our ability to operate together when it matters most,”

said Maj. Gen. Matthew T. Mowery, deputy commander, U.S. Marine Corps Forces, Pacific.

> “Bringing together four nations and six military services allows us to better align priorities, improve interoperability and campaign as a unified force under a shared plan. That cooperation strengthens our collective readiness and reinforces our commitment to a free and open Indo-Pacific.”

Pacific Land Forces Strengthen Cooperation During Land Forces Dialogue Technical Working Group in Sydney Photo by CPL Hamid Farahani

Senior leaders and delegation members from Australia, the United States, Japan and the Philippines attend an ice-breaker function at the Victoria Barracks Officers' Mess, Sydney, during the Land Force Dialogue – Technical Working Group on 17 November 2026. *** Local Caption *** Senior military leaders and delegates participating in the Land Force Dialogue – Technical Working Group attended an ice-breaker function at Victoria Barracks, Sydney, ahead of formal discussions. The function provided an opportunity for delegates from Australia, the United States, Japan and the Philippines to build professional relationships and discuss shared security interests. The Land Force Dialogue – Technical Working Group serves as a key forum for participating land forces to strengthen cooperation and improve synchronisation of future operations, activities and investments throughout the Indo-Pacific region.

The Land Forces Dialogue provides a forum for sustained engagement on shared military priorities. The dialogue enables participating nations to coordinate campaign activities, align operational priorities and identify opportunities for future cooperation.

Participants reaffirmed their commitment to synchronize multilateral training objectives, increase operational effectiveness and enhance crisis-response capabilities. By building on established relationships and routine multinational training opportunities, the four nations continue to advance practical military cooperation and strengthen their ability to respond to shared security challenges.

The United States International Trade Commission.
Request for comments regarding International Trade Commission's Economic Analysis, Investigation No. MISC-054.
Pursuant to Section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930, the United States International Trade Commission (Commission) is seeking information from the public on its economic analysis, including its methodology and areas of focus.
To ensure consideration, written comments must be submitted on or before March 25, 2027.
Lisa R. Barton, Secretary to the Commission, U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Washington, DC 20436, telephone 202-205-2595. General information concerning the Commission may be obtained by accessing its internet server at https://www.usitc.gov. Hearing-impaired persons are advised that information can be obtained by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal on (202) 205-1810.
You may submit comments, identified by docket number MISC-054, by any of the following methods:
Agency Website: https://www.usitc.gov. You may submit comments on the Commission's electronic docket (EDIS) at https://edis.usitc.gov. For help accessing EDIS, please email EDIS3Help@usitc.gov.
Email: Submit comments via to Secretary@usitc.gov. Include docket ( printed page 76266) number MISC-054 in the subject line of the message. Comments submitted by email must be: in letter format and double-spaced (unless the document is less than two (2) pages); in portable document format (PDF); and signed with either a typed or written signature. All comments received will be posted without change to the agency's public record, including any personal information provided.
Instructions: All submissions received must include the agency name and docket number (MISC-054, along with written comments addressing the topics on which the USITC seeks information. All comments received will be posted without change to https://www.usitc.gov, including any personal information provided. Written comments filed on EDIS must conform to the provisions of section 201.8 of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure (19 CFR 201.8).
Docket: For access to the docket to read background documents or comments received, go to https://www.usitc.gov and/or the U.S. International Trade Commission, 500 E Street SW, Room 112, Washington, DC 20436.
Jennifer Andberg, Office of External Relations ((202) 205-3404, or Jennifer.Andberg@usitc.gov). Hearing-impaired individuals may obtain information on this matter by contacting the Commission's TDD terminal at 202-205-1810. General information about the Commission is available by accessing the Commission website at www.usitc.gov. Persons with mobility impairments who will need special assistance in gaining access to the Commission should contact the Office of the Secretary at (202) 205-2000.
1. Relevant Statutory Authorities
Pursuant to section 332 of the Tariff Act of 1930 (19 U.S.C. 1332 (“section 332”)), whenever requested, the Commission submits to the President, and, by delegation, the United States Trade Representative (USTR); the Senate Finance Committee (SFC); or the House Ways and Means Committee (HWM) information and analysis on any matter related to tariffs, international trade, and industry competitiveness. Additionally, the President or Congress can task the Commission with factfinding investigations on various topics, which the Commission can also institute on its own initiative. Other statutes such as section 131 of the Trade Act of 1974 and statutes for specific trade agreements also provide authority to conduct factfinding investigations.
The Commission's work under section 332 and these other authorities utilize some degree of economic analysis. In such investigations, the Commission often analyzes the ways that trade and trade policy affect U.S. workers, producers, consumers, and the U.S. economy as a whole. The analysis helps inform policymakers' decisions on trade policy and international trade negotiations. In conjunction with other factfinding tools such as public hearings and written submissions, the Commission often uses analytical approaches including quantitative models, which are simplified, mathematical representations of an economy or industry using certain real-world data, to help isolate—and thereby understand—the impact of a past or future change when many factors could affect the outcomes.
To ensure that the Commission can meet the challenges posed by changing global and economic circumstances that are highly relevant to trade, it has decided to evaluate on an ongoing basis its analytical tools, data sources, and methodologies to ensure its work remains accurate, relevant, and responsive to its stakeholders.
2. Commission Analytical Approaches and How They Are Used
Given the variety of topics the Commission is obligated to analyze, the Commission uses a variety of analytical techniques, which can be combined to suit the topic(s) to be examined, including qualitative analysis, quantitative analysis without modeling, and quantitative analysis with economic modeling, which, as mentioned, can help assess the impact of a policy change by filtering out other factors, with important caveats.
The Commission's models vary by technique and scope. Major simulation models are built at the level of an industry or the entire economy. At the economy-wide level, the main modeling approach at the Commission has historically been the computable general equilibrium (CGE) model, based on the Global Trade Analysis Project (GTAP) database. This approach has been deployed numerous times in both factfinding investigations, such as in the evaluation of the likely impact of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) that the Commission published in 2019 (Inv. No. TPA-105-003, U.S.-Mexico-Canada Trade Agreement: Likely Impact on the U.S. Economy and on Specific Industry Sectors). Meanwhile, industry-level partial equilibrium models focus on a single economic sector without modeling the interactions between economic sectors, such as in the Commission's regular assessments of the USMCA automotive rules of origin (Inv. No. 332-600, USMCA Automotive Rules of Origin: Economic Impact and Operation, 2025 Report).
Although less frequently deployed in factfinding investigations as stand-alone models, econometric models have been used, for example, to measure the extent of “pass-through” from tariffs to U.S. prices in the Commission's analysis of the impact of the tariffs imposed in 2023 under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962 and section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 (Inv. No. 332-591, Economic Impact of Section 232 and 301 Tariffs on U.S. Industries). More recently, in place of a CGE model, the Commission used an econometric “gravity” equation as part of a general equilibrium gravity model in a 2026 study on the impact of revoking China's permanent normal trade relations status (Inv. No. 330-609, Effects on the U.S. Economy of Revoking China's Permanent Normal Trade Relations Status).
In addition to the above trade models that have generally been focused on medium- and long-run outcomes, such as by assuming the entire U.S. labor force is employed and can move freely across sectors, the Commission is considering how to develop and deploy economic models that are more equipped to look at short-term outcomes before employment, wages and other aspects of the economy fully adjust to any policy change.
Because models cannot capture every feature of the real world, they necessarily rely on assumptions and simplifications. Different modeling approaches may also emphasize different channels through which policies affect economic outcomes. Economy-wide simulation models, such as CGE models, have been subject to criticism regarding certain assumptions, including assumptions about full employment and worker mobility across sectors, particularly when used to analyze the effects of trade policy changes.
II. Topics on Which USITC Seeks Information
The Commission seeks information from the public on any of the following topics. After the comment period concludes, the Commission intends to produce a report that includes a summary of comments. The comments will also inform how the Commission moves forward with its factfinding Section 332 and related responsibilities. ( printed page 76267)
1. Do you think the Commission currently has the right analytical tools, including economic models, to address major trade policy questions over the next 5-10 years? Why or why not?
a. What non-modeling approaches should the Commission's analytical toolkit include?
b. What is the full suite of models ( e.g., industry-specific versus economy-wide; short-term versus long-term) that the Commission should have available for use in its analysis?
2. What factors or topics should the Commission's economic analysis be able to consider? Would they include, but not be limited to, the following:
a. Effect of trade on labor markets
i. Short-term effect on workers
ii. Long-term effect on workers ( e.g., changes in workforce capacity or skill sets in certain industries)
iii. Effect on the quality of jobs available for workers, including any shifts in wages, benefits, or job security
b. Effect of trade on investment
c. Effect of hostile trade actions, including boycotts, export controls, or other trade sanctions placed on the United States or U.S. persons
d. Effect of trade on distribution of wealth/income within the United States, including across geographic regions and demographic groups
e. Effect of trade on the environment
f. Effect of trade on immigration
g. Interaction of trade policy with domestic policies and regulations ( e.g. intellectual property, environmental regulations, labor regulations, tax policy, immigration policy)
h. Interaction of trade with domestic and international protection and enforcement of intellectual property rights
i. Interaction with trade imbalances
j. Interaction with market concentration
k. Other topics you believe would be useful for the Commission to consider
3. Given the Commission's statutory obligations, which of the above topics should the Commission prioritize?
4. Please discuss what trade questions are well suited to modeling, and which are better served by a different sort of analysis, such as descriptive trend analysis, legal analysis, or other analytical approaches.
5. How effective have the Commission's models been at evaluating the effects of major trade policy changes in past years? Please reference specific examples.
6. How can the Commission best engage in quality control of its modeling prospectively and evaluate the accuracy of its modeling retrospectively? Should the Commission regularly and publicly undertake model validation to evaluate the accuracy of its models?
7. Are there existing alternatives to Commission models that are more accurate, or that would capture factors that the Commission should consider? What trade-offs, if any, might such other models have?
8. Are there other branches of economics or disciplines outside of economics that might be useful in helping the Commission improve its modeling and other analytical techniques? Please provide specific examples of techniques, papers, authors, or other details to help the Commission identify these items.
9. How can the Commission incorporate or improve any of the following practices, and are there examples of best practices from a Commission report or external report:
a. Sensitivity analysis to test the importance of assumptions on model outcomes
b. Indications as to the level of certainty of model estimates
c. Plain narrative explanation and data visualization
d. Transparency of model assumptions and limitations
e. Replicability of model releases
10. Should the Commission attempt to quantify the impact of nontariff measures (NTMs) on trade? If quantification is appropriate, how should this be conducted? How should the Commission account for the potential non-trade-related impacts of NTMs ( e.g., on public health and the environment)?
11. What datasets should be created, refined, or expanded upon for the Commission's use on understanding the effects of trade policy?
12. How can the Commission make the best use of AI tools for quantitative analysis?
13. Are there any ways in which the Commission's information-gathering techniques such as public hearings, field visits, written submission periods, or surveys can be improved?
14. From whom ( e.g., the public and/or technical experts) should the Commission receive input regarding its analytical approaches, and with what frequency and in what manner should the Commission solicit such input? Would the Commission benefit from establishing a public advisory council for economic modeling?
15. Anything else that the submitter believes would help the Commission improve its modeling.
III. Submission Instructions
Written submissions: Interested persons are invited to file written submissions and other information concerning the matters to be addressed in this request. All written submissions should be addressed to the Secretary, and should be received no later than 5:15 p.m., March 25, 2027. All written submissions must conform to the provisions of section 201.8 of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure (19 CFR 201.8). Filings must be made through the Commission's Electronic Document Information System (EDIS, https://edis.usitc.gov) or via email. Persons with questions regarding electronic filing should contact the Office of the Secretary, Docket Services Division (202-205-1802), email EDIS3help@usitc.gov, or consult the Commission's Handbook on Filing Procedures.
Any submissions that contain confidential business information (CBI) must also conform with the requirements in section 201.6 of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure (19 CFR 201.6). Section 201.6 of the rules requires that the cover of the document and the individual pages be clearly marked as to whether they are the “confidential” or “nonconfidential” version, and that the CBI is clearly identified by means of brackets. All written submissions, except for CBI, will be made available for inspection by interested persons.
All information, including CBI, submitted may be disclosed to and used: (i) by the Commission, its employees and Offices, and contract personnel (a) for developing or maintaining the records of this or a related proceeding, or (b) in internal investigations, audits, reviews, and evaluations relating to the programs, personnel, and operations of the Commission including under 5 U.S.C. Appendix 3; or (ii) by U.S. government employees and contract personnel for cybersecurity or other security purposes. The Commission will not otherwise disclose any CBI in a manner that would reveal the operations of the firm supplying the information.
By order of the Commission.

# EU says 'strongly' rejects premise of new US tariffs

Issued on: 25/11/2026 - 20:48 Modified: 25/11/2026 - 20:54

Share

The EU said Wednesday that it rejected the premise of new tariffs on its exports proposed by the United States and expected Washington to stick by a deal struck with Brussels last year. The US unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies including the European Union and China, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production. FRANCE 24's Dave Keating reports from Brussels.

title: Jensen Huang is back, but China’s AI chip crunch is far from over
zh_title: 黄仁勋回来了，但中国的人工智能芯片危机还远未结束
summary: 美国限制措施后，中国人工智能芯片紧缩加剧海峡时报 黄仁勋回来了，但中国的人工智能芯片危机还远未结束 现在就注册：深入了解亚洲的快速发展 中国的人工智能行业知道，它不能再依靠黄仁勋来帮助确保获得英伟达的先进芯片。发布于 2026 年 11 月 25 日晚上 9:40 更新于 2026 年 11 月 25 日晚上 10:53 美国新规将限制中国获得先进芯片和海外数据中心，可能会减缓人工智能模型的开发 腾讯和阿里巴巴等中国公司警告称，中国正在推动的扩张计划将被推迟并可能被削减

美国限制措施后，中国人工智能芯片紧缩加剧海峡时报
黄仁勋回来了，但中国的人工智能芯片危机还远未结束
立即注册：深入了解亚洲的快速发展
中国的人工智能行业知道，它不能再依靠黄仁勋来帮助确保获得英伟达的先进芯片。
发表于 2026 年 11 月 25 日，晚上 09:40
更新于 2026 年 11 月 25 日 10:53
美国新规定将限制中国获得先进芯片和海外数据中心，可能会减缓人工智能模型的开发
腾讯和阿里巴巴等中国公司警告称，扩张计划将被推迟并可能被削减
中国正在加大自力更生力度，但国产芯片仍落后
新加坡/北京 — — 黄仁勋可能会重新执掌英伟达，但他的回归并没有给依赖美国先进芯片的中国人工智能公司带来什么喘息的机会。
分析人士表示，11 月 19 日生效的美国新规定使中国企业更难从海外数据中心租用计算能力，从而在短期内对中国人工智能的发展造成重大挫折。
但这些限制措施可能会给中国多年来推动技术自力更生的努力增添新的紧迫性，将企业曾经视为后备计划的开发本土芯片和计算系统变成优先事项。
中国的人工智能行业知道，它不能再依赖黄仁勋来帮助确保获得英伟达的先进芯片。 11 月 23 日恢复担任首席执行官的黄仁勋曾是华盛顿最强烈主张继续向中国销售芯片的人之一。
新加坡南洋理工大学经济学名誉教授陈光炎表示：“对中国来说，最重要的教训是，它不能依赖个别美国企业领导人的善意，无论他们的商业影响力或与中国接触的意愿如何。”
总部位于华盛顿的咨询公司亚洲集团 (The Asia Group) 负责数字业务的合伙人乔治·陈 (George Chen) 指出，英伟达董事会已经成立了一个新委员会，负责监督国家安全风险和出口管制合规情况。
“英伟达肯定会在合规方面加倍努力，因为它不想再次被指责与中国过于亲密，”陈告诉海峡时报。
美国商务部工业与安全局11月16日宣布的新规定禁止美国境外的数据中心为具有强大计算能力的中国客户提供服务，除非获得美国政府许可。
由于远程访问占中国公司人工智能计算能力的近三分之一，科技巨头已经警告称，美国的限制可能会扰乱他们的计划。
腾讯表示，先进计算能力的减少可能会延长开发下一代混元人工智能模型所需的时间。腾讯总裁刘炽平在 11 月 18 日的财报电话会议上表示：“这让中国的每个人都感到沮丧。”
一天后，阿里巴巴首席执行官埃迪·吴表示，该公司可能会缩减其长期数据中心扩张目标。
这种不确定性也影响到了贷方。银行家已暂停一项拟议的 4.8 亿美元（6.2 亿新元）贷款，该贷款旨在支付马来西亚数据中心的 Nvidia 芯片费用，该数据中心将为 TikTok 的中国所有者字节跳动提供服务。
马来亚银行投资银行集团香港和中国股市首席研究策略师 Benjamin Ho 指出，在美国新的限制措施下，至少两家 Nvidia 的服务器合作伙伴暂停了向东南亚客户的交付。
